views.modern_french:
Colorno, ce 6 juillet 1760. Madame ma chère Sœur, c'est avec un plaisir inexprimable que j'ai reçu votre lettre. Comme je suis transportée par l'amitié que vous m'y témoignez ! Vous avez raison de réclamer la mienne désormais : elle est vôtre pour plusieurs raisons, et je vous assure, sans le moindre compliment, qu'elle est très sincère. J'espère que lorsque vous me connaîtrez, vous verrez combien je vous aime. Ce que je puis vous assurer, c'est que c'est de tout mon cœur ; mais vous en jugerez mieux par vous-même que je ne saurais vous l'exprimer. Mes sentiments sont trop forts pour que qui que ce soit puisse, quelle qu'éloquence il possède — et j'en suis bien éloignée —, les décrire dans toute leur étendue.

Vous me faites la joie, ma chère Sœur, de m'apprendre par votre première lettre la victoire remportée par le général Laudon sur un corps de Prussiens. C'est pour moi tout le bonheur à la fois. Il ne me suffisait pas de recevoir une lettre d'une personne qui m'est déjà si chère d'avance — il fallait encore qu'elle m'annonce une victoire complète. J'en étais hors de moi. C'est avec justice que vous jugez de la part que j'ai prise à cette heureuse nouvelle. Il ne pouvait en être autrement, car je ne me considère que comme Allemande et mon cœur l'est parfaitement, je vous l'assure. Je le dois par gratitude et par les liens qui m'uniront à une famille adorable, mais de plus ce sentiment m'est naturel.

Adieu, ma chère Sœur, conservez-moi votre amitié, c'est tout ce que je désire ; mais je vous en supplie, n'ayez pas si bonne opinion de moi — sauf pour ce qui concerne ma tendresse —, car vous devrez y renoncer furieusement quand vous me connaîtrez. Soyez assurée que je suis et serai toute ma vie votre fidèle sœur Isabelle Marie Louise.

views.literal_english_modern:
Colorno, July sixth, seventeen sixty. Madam, my dear Sister — it is with inexpressible pleasure that I received your letter. How moved I am by the friendship you show me there! You are right to lay claim to mine from now on. It belongs to you for several reasons, and I assure you, without the least flattery, that it is entirely sincere. I hope that when you come to know me, you will see how much I love you. What I can tell you is that it is with all my heart — though you will judge that better for yourself than I could ever put into words. My feelings are too strong for anyone to describe in their full extent, whatever eloquence they may possess, and I possess very little.

You give me the joy, my dear Sister, of learning through your very first letter of the victory won by General Laudon over a body of Prussians. It is all happiness for me at once. It was not enough that I should receive a letter from someone already so dear to me — she had also to bring news of a complete victory, and I was quite beside myself. You judge rightly of the share I took in this happy news. It could not have been otherwise, for I think of myself only as German, and my heart is perfectly so, I assure you. I owe this feeling to gratitude and to the bonds that will unite me with an adorable family, but beyond that it is simply natural to me.

Farewell, my dear Sister. Keep your friendship for me — that is all I ask. But please do not think too well of me, except where my tenderness is concerned, for you would have to revise that opinion sharply once you know me. Be assured that I am, and shall be all my life, your faithful sister, Isabelle Marie Louise.
views.plain_english:
Colorno, July 6, 1760. My dearest Sister — I can't begin to describe the joy I felt on receiving your letter. The warmth you show me there! You are right to ask for my friendship in return: it is yours, truly and sincerely, with no flattery intended. When you know me better, I think you'll see how deeply I mean it. My feelings go beyond what words can capture — certainly beyond what my own limited eloquence can express.

And what a gift you gave me with your very first letter — news of General Laudon's victory over the Prussians! It was almost too much happiness at once. Not only did I hear from someone already so dear to me, but the letter brought word of a complete victory. I was absolutely beside myself with joy. You were right to suppose I would care deeply about such news. How could I not? I think of myself as German through and through, and my heart truly is. I feel it out of gratitude and because of the bonds that will tie me to a wonderful family — but honestly, it also just comes naturally to me.

Farewell, dear Sister. Keep your friendship for me — that is all I want. Only don't think too highly of me, except when it comes to my love for you, because you'll have to change your mind pretty sharply once you know me better! Know that I am, and always will be, your devoted sister, Isabelle Marie Louise.

views.plain_english:
Colorno, July 26, 1760. My dearest Sister — your letters always seem to arrive with good news. Two in a row now, each with word of a new victory! I hope that when the third comes, the King of Prussia will be finished off completely. I'd dearly like that, because it might finally bring us peace. How wonderful it would be if peace were at least in the air by the time I arrive — though even that hope doesn't run as deep as the interest your friendship stirs in me for everything that touches you, and above all for Her Majesty the Empress, for whom I feel the most sincere gratitude and affection.

You'll never convince me, dear Sister, that I deserve all the warmth you feel for me. What I can say is that my love for you does deserve it. And I promise you that beyond the bond we will soon share through family ties, I already feel for you everything a true sister and a devoted friend could feel. But I must also gently scold you for selling yourself so short. Believe me, in every way you deserve the love of everyone lucky enough to know you, whether in person or by reputation.

And you can absolutely count on me being a good Austrian — and then some. Your faithful sister.

We almost never actually play together — and when we do, it's either passages that have to be played connected, which doesn't work, or passages played separately, which are too strong for the harpsichord and end up making it sound harsh and jarring. I'll do my best to accompany, but it's tricky because the bow's leap is never as precise as the harpsichord. Anyway, I can run it through with you on the first day and you can decide for yourself. Enseignez-moi ma faute, je vous en supplie, afin que je puisse la corriger — afin que j'aie le temps de la laver dans mes larmes toute une nuit, larmes de regret d'avoir pu outrager l'objet le plus aimable, le plus chéri. Enseignez-la moi, dis-je, si vous ne voulez apprendre demain à votre réveil que le malheureux Zerbin, par un tour du sort, n'existe plus ; qu'il est mort sans regretter la vie, mort de désespoir de votre cruauté, et que même en enfer où son désespoir le précipite, il vivra pour vous aimer, que son plus grand tourment sera là votre tyrannie. Mais vous n'en viendrez pas là. Vous connaissez trop mon cœur pour ne pas craindre des résolutions trop outrageantes ; vous me consolerez donc, vous me rendrez la vie, et nous nous embrasserons de nouveau demain. Adieu, mais hâtez-vous de me tirer de l'état où je suis, car autrement, adieu.

Tout écrit, en grand et en petit, je ne puis rien faire — et même les charmes de la Bentinck que je verrai demain ne pourront frapper ma vue. Adieu Eserl, je vous adore, je trinque et je vous embrasse. Au reste, je vous ai envoyé quatre péchés, mais ne croyez pas que ce soit pour tenter de vous adoucir — je ne vous sais pas de pareils sentiments bas, et les miens en sont trop loin.

Non, mein Engerl, c'est seulement par mes sentiments que j'entends vous ramener.

[Notes : 1. Laurette et Zerbin sont des amants de comédie. 2. Charlotte Sophie, comtesse von Bentinck von Réne, née comtesse von Aldenburg (1715–1800). Elle séjourna à Vienne de décembre 1758 à fin septembre 1761. 3. « Petit âne. » 4. Confirme que c'est l'été. 5. « Mon petit ange. »]

I would rather die of suspense than fail to get what I am about to ask of you. My dear Laurette — is this really what you had planned for the third day of our marriage? Can you watch in perfect calm while at your feet there expires a lover, a husband, a sister, a friend — honestly, the most devoted friend you have? An innocent soul who never imagined doing anything to upset you, who lies waiting for your verdict, who only wants to know what he did wrong so he can make it right, even at the cost of his own blood? Please, tell me my fault. Let me correct it. Let me spend the whole night washing it away with tears — tears of shame at having hurt the most wonderful, most beloved person in the world. Tell me, I beg you — unless you want to wake up tomorrow and learn that poor Zerbin, by some cruel stroke of fate, is no more; that he died without a single regret for life, killed by the despair your cruelty has caused; that even in hell, whither his despair will have hurled him, he will still love you, and his worst torment will be your tyranny. But you would never let it come to that. You know my heart too well to risk pushing me over the edge. You will comfort me, bring me back to life, and tomorrow we will be in each other's arms again. Farewell — but please hurry, and save me from this agony. Otherwise, it really is goodbye.

I have written everything out, large and small, and still I am helpless. Even the charms of the Countess Bentinck, whom I am to see tomorrow, cannot reach me. Farewell, Eserl — I adore you, I drink to you, I kiss you. Oh, and I sent you four little sweetmeats — not as a bribe, I promise. I would never credit you with such petty feelings, and I am above them myself.

No, my little angel — it is my love alone that I am counting on to bring you back to me.

[Eserl is a Viennese German pet name meaning "little donkey"; mein Engerl means "my little angel." The Countess von Bentinck was a prominent visitor to Vienna at the time. Laurette and Zerbin are names from Italian comic opera, which Isabelle uses to dramatise her own feelings.]

How can I face you, dear Sister, after all I have done? I admit I lost my temper and said things I should not have, in the heat of the moment. I beg you, by everything you hold dear: be fair to me and acknowledge my love, or put it to the test — ask whatever you want of me, however hard, and I will do it gladly, if only it can change your mind. You have misunderstood me, and it is breaking my heart. If nothing can convince you, just say so. You will always find me ready to be honest with you. I will not give up on you — but I will at least try to be worthy of your regret for losing me, since it seems I am no longer worthy of your friendship.

Summer, 1761, 1762, or 1763

Summer — year uncertain

I am afraid I will not be able to get away as I promised. Something has had me in its grip and not let me breathe for a moment. So — is our three o'clock meeting still on? Farewell.

Farewell, I embrace you and kiss you with all my heart. The tennis game is underway. be together all day while the Empress will be at Colloredo's, and that's the day after tomorrow. Farewell, I kiss you, give me your orders and they will surely be carried out to the letter. 1. Count Rodolphe de Colloredo [1706-1788] was vice-chancellor of court and state. views.modern_french:
Fin d'été – automne 1761

Je vous avais promis qu'il ferait beau aujourd'hui — je tiens parole. Mais j'ai malheureusement été obligée de m'adresser à Éole pour chasser la pluie, et à l'enchaîné Borée, à qui il ne restait plus la moindre maîtrise. Plus de joie, moins de plaisir — tout s'ennuie, on ne peut espérer rien de mieux que la tristesse et la douleur ; les choses les plus agréables perdent leur substance. Même la musique, seule consolation de tous les êtres, ne suffit plus à remettre à leur place les idées désorientées. Que devons-nous entreprendre dans ce besoin désespéré ? Quand on est triste, on ne trouve de meilleur réconfort que dans de saintes et mélancoliques lectures. J'ai pourtant trouvé un remède pour me consoler : la société, la musique — en vain. Je me suis appliquée à la chasse. Si vous veillez à ce que le temps soit beau demain, tout est réglé.

Adieu, je vous embrasse et vous baise de tout mon cœur. La partie de tennis est en cours. Être ensemble toute la journée pendant que l'Impératrice sera chez Colloredo, c'est pour après-demain. Adieu, je vous embrasse — donnez-moi vos ordres et ils seront assurément exécutés à la lettre.

[Note : Le comte Rodolphe de Colloredo (1706–1788) était vice-chancelier de cour et d'État. Il dirigeait les services de la chancellerie impériale à Vienne.]

Late summer to autumn, 1761

I had promised you fine weather today, and I am keeping my word — though unfortunately I was obliged to call upon Aeolus to drive away the rain, and upon a chained Boreas who had long since lost any hold on calm. No joy, no pleasure — everything turns grey. One can hope for nothing better than sadness and pain; the most agreeable things lose their savour. Even music, the sole comfort of all living souls, is no longer enough to settle one's scattered thoughts in their proper place. What is to be done in such desperate need? When one is sorrowful, one finds no better comfort than in grave and melancholy reading. And yet I found a remedy: society, music — all in vain. I turned to hunting. If you can arrange for the weather to be fine tomorrow, all will be well.

Farewell — I embrace and kiss you with all my heart. The tennis game is under way. Being together all day while the Empress is at Colloredo's will be the day after tomorrow. Farewell, I kiss you. Give me your orders and they shall certainly be carried out to the letter.

[Count Rodolphe de Colloredo, seventeen oh six to seventeen eighty-eight, served as vice-chancellor of court and state and headed the imperial chancellery in Vienna.]
views.plain_english:
Late summer to autumn, 1761

I promised you fine weather today, and I am keeping that promise — though I confess I had to call in a few mythological favours to hold back the rain, with limited success. The gloom has settled in: no joy, no pleasure, everything flat. There is nothing to look forward to but sadness and pain, and even the most pleasant things have lost their appeal. Even music — the one true comfort for any suffering soul — is no longer enough to quiet the mind's restless wanderings. What is one to do when things are this desperate? I suppose in low spirits there is nothing better than serious, melancholy reading. Yet even that failed me. I tried company, I tried music — useless. I took up hunting. If you can guarantee fine weather tomorrow, everything will be fine.

Farewell — I hug and kiss you with all my heart. The tennis game is already going. We are to spend the whole day together while the Empress visits Colloredo's — that is the day after tomorrow. Farewell, I kiss you. Tell me what you need and consider it done.

[Count Colloredo was vice-chancellor of the imperial court in Vienna, and one of its most powerful administrators.]

views.original_french: February 1762 Hello, adorable Sister. Until I myself can have the pleasure of going to your house, I cannot help writing to you, especially since I believe that it is easier for me to talk to you in writing than in speech about things that I cannot communicate to anyone other than you. I still have a good reason for taking this course, it is that my chest is still too exhausted from yesterday to dare risk a long speech. Besides, when we see you, we can only be occupied with your charms, and all the most beautiful ideas give way to the desire to kiss. This is a start that will undoubtedly annoy you, because you don't like sweets, but also it's the last such statement of the day, which should console you and prove to you that at twenty you are the master of your passions. I implore you not to let what I told you yesterday about the LL [?] leak out, otherwise nothing would work and we would miss the opportunity that is so dear to your heart, especially with regard to my sister Marie-Anne. Take good care of yourself. For the rest, take care of my sister Marie-Anne, because I cannot hide from you that we will still have some scenes on the first day, I would be sorry, but even more so if you found yourself involved in it perhaps without knowing it. Besides the train she did 1 recently with the Lehner, I know very well that she writes to the Princess. Perhaps this is false, I hope so, but it is certain that she bragged about it. I am convinced that it is nothing but very innocent, but you know the defenses. The Empress Vignore; If she finds out, she will be furious. La Vasquez doesn't want to believe it, so don't talk to her about it, I wouldn't tell you if I wasn't afraid that you might be accused of having had a part in it. So flee, in the name of God, any conversation with my sister Marie-Anne, do not appear to be trying to speak to her because even moving away from everyone, perhaps inadvertently without perhaps saying anything to her, would give rise to suspicion. At the end, when you return from the Empress with her, make sure that a maid follows you until you are each at your own place. It's not that I believe you capable of doing anything wrong, but if the slightest complaint were raised against her, so that you would have proof in hand for everything that could happen. Precautions are always good. Forgive me for my worries, I love you too much not to have them when I fear that someone will play some bad trick on you. Goodbye, I am going to get dressed to go to your house or I hope we can speak even more clearly. 1. Unidentified person.
views.modern_french:
Février 1762

Bonjour, adorable Sœur. En attendant d'avoir moi-même le plaisir d'aller chez vous, je ne puis m'empêcher de vous écrire — d'autant plus que je crois qu'il m'est plus aisé de vous parler par écrit que de vive voix de choses que je ne puis communiquer à d'autres qu'à vous. J'ai encore une bonne raison de prendre ce parti : c'est que ma poitrine est encore trop épuisée d'hier pour oser risquer un long discours. D'ailleurs, quand on vous voit, on ne peut être occupée que de vos charmes, et les plus belles idées cèdent au désir d'embrasser. C'est un début qui vous importunera sans doute, car vous n'aimez pas les douceurs — mais c'est aussi le dernier aveu de ce genre de la journée, ce qui devrait vous consoler et vous prouver qu'à vingt ans on est maître de ses passions.

Je vous conjure de ne pas laisser transpirer ce que je vous ai dit hier au sujet des L.L. [?], autrement rien ne marcherait et nous manquerions l'occasion qui vous est si chère au cœur, surtout en ce qui concerne ma sœur Marie-Anne. Prenez bien soin de vous.

Pour le reste, prenez garde à ma sœur Marie-Anne, car je ne puis vous cacher que nous aurons encore quelques scènes le premier jour — j'en serais fâchée, mais encore davantage si vous vous trouviez mêlée sans le savoir. Outre la démarche qu'elle a faite récemment avec le Lehner, je sais très bien qu'elle écrit à la Princesse. Cela est peut-être faux — je l'espère — mais il est certain qu'elle s'en est vantée. Je suis persuadée que c'est la chose la plus innocente du monde, mais vous savez les défenses. L'Impératrice l'ignore ; si elle l'apprend, elle sera furieuse. La Vasquez ne veut pas le croire — ne lui en parlez donc pas. Je ne vous le dirais pas si je ne craignais qu'on ne vous accuse d'y avoir eu part. Fuyez donc, au nom de Dieu, toute conversation avec ma sœur Marie-Anne ; ne paraissez pas chercher à lui parler, car même vous éloigner de tout le monde, peut-être par inadvertance sans peut-être lui rien dire, donnerait lieu à des soupçons. À la fin, quand vous revenez de chez l'Impératrice avec elle, faites en sorte qu'une femme de chambre vous suive jusqu'à ce que vous soyez chacune chez vous. Good day, my favourite [Gne]. You do me an unspeakable injustice in believing that I always forget everything — and I believe it is not forgetting to leave this piece of furniture at your rooms. Easter is coming up — the tenth of April. I was minding my own business when suddenly an unwelcome gust arrived with all the force of a storm god wanting to get out. I thought it was alone and meant to let it pass freely, but apparently your niece — who I imagine had been overeating at the fair — decided to add something extra. Luckily I managed to stop in time. I kiss your adorable backside, keeping mine well away from you since it is currently in rather a sorry state.

Good news for you today, dear Sister: I am doing well. The bad news is that you won't get to see me — because as usual, you're a creature of habit and anything new upsets you, so I thought I'd better warn you ahead of time.

views.modern_french:
Eckartsau, ce 18 juin 1762, à 7 heures du matin

Je me lève à l'instant, chère Sœur, et comme je ne sais pas encore à quelle heure le courrier sera dépêché, ni si j'aurai ensuite le temps de t'écrire, je prends les devants. Nous avons la messe à huit heures, puis nous allons à la chasse. Le souper d'hier était fort gai grâce au Peintre, qui n'a pas cessé d'en parler après, car nous sommes restés encore un moment. J'ai fait enrager les Palffy, ce qui m'a bien fait rire. J'aurais aimé en faire autant avec Trauttsmandorff mais, bien que très aimable, tu sais qu'elle n'est pas du goût de l'autre. Aussi, laissant de côté tout ce qui pourrait être sérieux, j'ai juré de ne dire que des folies tout le temps que je serai ici ; autrement les gens diront que je suis ennuyeuse, ce qui pourrait bien être vrai.

T'ayant quittée, je t'assure que j'ai les larmes aux yeux à tout moment, et tu sais que toi seule sais les faire couler et les arrêter. Adieu, comporte-toi bien, je t'en prie, surtout demain : commence par bannir l'embarras, car on ne peut pas du tout raisonner si l'on n'est pas calme. Adieu, j'embrasse Vasquez et mon cher Phénix des millions de fois de tout mon cœur. Mes compliments à ma sœur Élisabeth et à ma sœur Jeanne.

Devine où je vais ? Je ne veux pas te le dire ; si tu es assez maligne, tu ne l'ignoreras pas longtemps. Et quel bonheur m'attend ! Je dois aller à la chasse avec toi ; je vais m'enfermer dans une voiture avec l'objet le plus digne d'admiration — et je ne dis pas d'amour — c'est la monstrueuse Ogilvy. Tu peux juger de quelle joie c'est pour moi, et si cela surpasse le plaisir que j'aurais eu à voir courir un malheureux cerf !

Je t'envoie un cahier à décrire — ou plutôt je ne te l'envoie pas car j'en ai besoin pour la suite du chapitre. Dès qu'il sera entièrement terminé, je te l'enverrai, et toujours par chapitres. Cela revient au même et c'est plus commode pour moi, j'en conviens. Je me croyais malade hier soir, j'avais des coliques, des douleurs aux reins, mais j'ai très bien dormi et je me porte très bien à présent.
views.literal_english_old:
Eckartsau, this June 18, 1762, at seven o'clock in the morning

I am getting up at this very moment, dear Sister, and as I do not yet know at what hour the courier will be dispatched, nor whether I shall then have the time to write to you, I am writing ahead. We have Mass at eight o'clock, after which we go hunting. Supper yesterday was very merry, thanks to the Painter — who did not cease speaking of it after supper, as we stayed some time longer. I put the Palffy ladies into a fury, which made me laugh greatly. I should have liked to do as much with Trauttsmandorff but, though very amiable, you know she is not to everyone's taste. Thus, setting aside all that might tend to seriousness, I have sworn to say only mad things for the whole time I am here; otherwise people will say that I am dull, which might well be true.

Having left you, I can assure you that I have tears in my eyes at all moments, and you know that you alone know how to make them flow and to stop them. Farewell; conduct yourself well, I beg you, especially tomorrow — begin by banishing all embarrassment, for one cannot reason at all if one is not calm. Farewell; I kiss [Vasquez] and my dear Phoenix millions of times with all my heart. My compliments to my sister Elisabeth and my sister Jeanne.

Guess where I am going? I do not wish to tell you; if you are clever enough, you shall not long remain in ignorance. And what happiness awaits me! I am to go hunting with you — I am to shut myself up in a carriage with the object most worthy of admiration — and I do not say of love — which is the monstrous Ogilvy. You may judge what joy that is for me, and whether it surpasses what I should have felt watching an unfortunate deer run!

I am sending you a notebook to be described — or rather, I am not sending it to you, as I need it for the remainder of the chapter. As soon as it is entirely finished, I will send it to you, and always in chapters. It comes to the same thing and is more convenient for me, I admit. I thought myself ill yesterday evening — I had [coliques], pains in the kidneys — but I slept very well and am very well at present.

views.plain_english:
October 6, 1762

I'm writing first today, dear Sister — you'll have to catch up. I was on good form at the opera yesterday, completely swept up in the music, and I even managed the Schniirl without any trouble for a moment. It was terribly hot, though. You probably already know that I was seated between the Archduke and my brother Leopold — so you can hardly accuse me of being unfaithful to you. I'll admit that I couldn't have borne anyone else beside me, because I'd have been thinking all evening: "What has become of my dear Eurydice?" — and I would have wept like Orpheus at the mere thought that you are mortal.

Goodbye for now — a kiss from me. I'm off at eight to the wine cellar, where I expect I'll come back nicely rosy, and then I'll have news to share.

views.modern_french:
Jeudi 11 novembre 1762

Comme tout ce que tu veux arrive, le Conseil est demain et vendredi, conférence samedi, lundi la Saint-Léopold, mardi départ pour Eckartsau. Voilà l'emploi du temps.

On aime davantage les êtres de la même espèce quand ils sont supérieurs en puissance, et l'expérience récente de Schönbrunn a vérifié ma croyance. Il est aussi vrai qu'on aime parfois ses semblables quand ils sont soumis, tendres et respectueux. J'ai du moins toutes les raisons de l'espérer et j'ose même m'en flatter, étant moi aussi de l'espèce diabolique ou méchante. Bonheur sans pareil pour moi de pouvoir me comparer à ce que j'ai de plus cher au monde et à ce qui est le plus adorable.

Sur ce, j'ai l'honneur d'être, Madame, de Votre Altesse Royale — pour ranger toute ma bibliothèque ; elle est sens dessus dessous, et si vous voulez savoir en un mot ce qu'est ma tête, je peux la définir comme un fouillis de folie et de ténèbres, de méchanceté et de raison. Savez-vous le désordre qui règne dans un certain tiroir de chez moi ? On y trouve pêle-mêle et sans aucune raison un écrit politique, un paquet de lettres, un opéra comique, un vaudeville, un traité d'éducation, un jeu de clavecin, des réflexions morales, un sermon attaché au traité de toutes les déraisons, des prières mêlées à du papier consacré.

Il est néanmoins vrai que vous n'auriez pu vous adresser à quelqu'un qui ait votre personne et vos qualités plus vivement gravées dans le cœur que moi, ni qui vous aime plus tendrement. Aussi vais-je vous dire sincèrement ce que je pense de vous, et je vais commencer votre portrait par votre visage. Je vous dirai donc que je ne saurais imaginer rien de plus agréable. De beaux yeux, des cheveux de la même couleur, une jolie bouche, et avec tout cela tant de physionomie qu'on devine à travers vos airs avisés tout l'esprit que vous possédez. Une belle gorge et une taille qu'on ne saurait mieux faire.

Je vous reprocherais cependant d'être un peu trop prévenue contre ceux dont vous l'avez décidé, et vous n'en revenez pas aisément. Vous aimez à tourmenter, mais dès que vous avez atteint votre but de mettre les gens en colère, vous regrettez d'y avoir réussi. Permettez-moi de vous dire que ce grand désir de mort que vous montrez est un sentiment mal placé : c'est soit de l'amour-propre, soit le désir de paraître héroïque, car ce serait quelque chose que votre bon cœur contredirait s'il devait affliger les personnes qui vous sont vraiment attachées que vous leur teniez de tels discours.
views.literal_english_old:
Thursday, November 11, 1762

As everything you wish comes to pass, the Council is tomorrow and on Friday, conference on Saturday, Saint Leopold's day on Monday, departure for Eckartsau on Tuesday.

One loves beings of one's own species the more when they are superior in power, and the recent experience of Schönbrunn has verified my belief. It is also true that we sometimes love our fellow creatures when they are submissive, tender, and respectful. I have at least every reason to hope so, and I even venture to flatter myself on the point, being also of the diabolical or wicked species. What an unparalleled happiness for me to be able to compare myself to what I hold most dear in the world and to what is most adorable.

On this, I have the honour of being, Madam, of Your Royal Highness — to sort out my entire library, which is upside down; and if you wish to know in a word what my head is, I may define it as a jumble of madness and darkness, of wickedness and reason. Do you know the confusion that reigns in a certain drawer that dwells in my house? One finds there, all together and without rhyme or reason, a political treatise, a pile of letters, a comic opera, a vaudeville, a treatise on education, a harpsichord game, moral reflections, a sermon attached to a treatise on all manner of unreason, and prayers mingled with consecrated paper.

It is nevertheless true that you could not have addressed yourself to one who has your person and your qualities more keenly engraved upon their heart than I, nor who loves you more tenderly. I shall therefore tell you sincerely what I think of you, and I shall begin your portrait with your face. I shall say, then, that I cannot conceive of anything more pleasing. Beautiful eyes, hair of the same colour, a pretty mouth, and with all this so much [physiognomie] that one perceives through your knowing air all the [esprit] you possess. A beautiful throat and a figure that could not be improved upon.

I would nevertheless reproach you for being a little too set against those upon whom you have formed a design, and you do not easily return from it. You love to torment, but as soon as you have achieved your aim of making people angry, you are sorry to have succeeded. Allow me to tell you that this great desire for death which you display is a misplaced sentiment: it is either [amour-propre] or the desire to appear heroic — for it would be something your good heart would contradict, were it to distress those who are truly attached to you by giving them such speeches.

Thursday, November 11, 1762

As usual everything happens just as you want it: Council tomorrow and Friday, conference Saturday, Saint Leopold's day Monday, and off to Eckartsau on Tuesday.

I've come to believe we love people of our own kind most when they hold more power than us — and Schönbrunn recently proved me right about that. Though of course it's also true that we can love people when they are gentle, tender, and respectful. I have every reason to hope that is the case, and I flatter myself that it is — being myself of the diabolical and wicked variety. What a privilege it is for me to be able to compare myself to the dearest and most adorable person in the world.

On that note — I need to sort out my library, which is in complete chaos. If you want one word for the state of my mind, it would be this: a jumble of madness and darkness, of wickedness and reason. You should see the disorder in a certain drawer in my room: all thrown together with no logic whatsoever — a political essay, a heap of letters, a comic opera, a vaudeville, a treatise on education, a harpsichord piece, moral reflections, a sermon, prayers mixed in with consecrated paper.

You could not, however, have found anyone who loves you more sincerely or has you more deeply inscribed on their heart. So I am going to tell you exactly what I think of you and begin with your face. I cannot imagine anything more delightful: beautiful eyes, hair to match, a pretty mouth, and such an expressive face that you can read every spark of intelligence in it just from the way you look. A lovely neck and a figure that could not be improved upon.

My one criticism: once you've decided against someone, you hold that view firmly and it is nearly impossible to change your mind. You love to torment people — but the moment you succeed in making them angry, you're sorry about it. And please let me say: this great longing for death you keep expressing is quite misplaced. It's either vanity or a desire to seem dramatic, because your kind heart would never truly wish to cause such distress to those who love you.

I have forgotten everything I meant to tell you. Here I am, entirely at your service, and I am going to ask about the Mons — I hope you will be at the window, for I am not in the least mood for jokes. Farewell.

I can say that my sleep was longer, less broken, and more peaceful than it has been for a very long time. Tell me how you are and whether you too have slept. Farewell; I kiss you and am on my way as well.

Here I am, thoroughly saturated with it all — and since whatever I might have tried, I found neither another shirt, nor stockings, nor clothes, the despair of missing such a happy moment woke me up. Yet I was not entirely wrong to have dreamed I was feverish, for I have just now observed a slight tendency in that direction, though still quite distant. I flatter myself that Vasquez had a successful hunt last night. The weather at least seemed disposed to grant him that pleasure; my fear is that it did not last.

Farewell. Do not worry — it is not worth it. I trust you will see clearly and not hide anything from yourself. But I won't praise you too much given all the stories we tell each other. And above all, don't mention any of this to Van Swieten, who is in a foul temper trying to work out what is wrong. Farewell again; I kiss you and await your note with all the impatience in the world.

By the way — I am enclosing a small orange-peel biscuit, which will be very good for clearing the taste of the medicinal decoctions if you eat it afterwards.

End of February — beginning of March 1763

I can't thank you enough for your sweet note, dear Sister. You are too kind, wanting to give me news of your health when I'm not happy with it at all. As for me, I was quite ill last night after Van Swieten left — as if the devil had arranged things on purpose so Van Swieten couldn't see what was wrong. I slept badly, tossed and turned, had dreadful dreams, and was hit by a wave of complete exhaustion. I'm fine now though. I'll come to you as soon as I can and arrange my dinner to suit you. Goodbye, dear Sister — I embrace you with everything I have.

The prunes helped — I slept reasonably well, but woke up coughing for what must have been a quarter of an hour. In truth it was laziness not to get up sooner, because the moment I ate a bit of marshmallow paste it stopped immediately. Tell me how you are — I always send you my love. Good morning, and a hello to Vasquez.

Tu seras surprise, chère Sœur, de recevoir ce billet à ton réveil, et tu penseras soit que je suis de très bonne heure, soit que je t'écris avant d'aller à confesse. Ni l'un ni l'autre.

views.plain_english:
Early March 1763

You'll be surprised to find this note waiting for you this morning, dear Sister — you'll think either that I'm up at the crack of dawn or that I'm writing before confession. Neither, actually.

I coughed, fell back asleep, woke again, coughed, got up, then coughed some more. Yet I really am doing quite well — though my sleep still worries me, so please don't mention it to anyone. Goodbye for now; I kiss you. If there is a tennis match and I can manage it, I'll let you know — or I'll simply come round. Tell me what works best for you. A million kisses.

Oh, and Prince Albert is doing better — how very helpful of me to report that. We'll see each other this afternoon: there's a card game at the Empress's and I've been invited. In the meantime, all my love. Please kiss Vasquez for me and let Countess Daun and Countess Lynden know I'd love them to come and play at my place this evening after seven.

Please tell me every single day, exactly how you are. It is my only consolation and I could not live without it. Goodbye — I kiss you and adore you more than I can say, to such a degree that the smallest inconvenience on your part makes me afraid for your life.

views.original_french: March 1763 I am sorry for the time I will have to spend without seeing you. It broke my heart so much that I almost started crying. I will try to console myself by writing to you as often as I can. I am still delighted that it is in these times that you have it, where we are almost always at church, although you could still have waited until Thursday, at least I will not be in bad company. Erdédy puts herself at your feet and tells you that she is in a very bad mood. I am no less so and I think I was yesterday out of a presentiment. The Archduke makes you say “very good, you must be ashamed to stay in good health”. Goodbye, fuck you waiting 2 until I catch it too and can actually do it. 1. Vienna Political Correspondence, vol. 294, f. 100 v., March 26, 1763: “Archduchess Marie [Christine], second daughter of the Empress, with measles declared two days ago. » 2. If Silsabelle had had measles, she could have continued to see Marie-Christine.
views.modern_french:
Mars 1763

Je suis ravie, chère Sœur, que tu aies dormi. Je n'avais aucun doute que la visite de l'Impératrice te ferait du bien. Je suis désolée pour toi de la tristesse dans laquelle je me trouverai — et désolée pour le temps que je devrai passer sans te voir. Cela m'a brisé le cœur au point que j'ai failli commencer à pleurer. J'essaierai de me consoler en t'écrivant aussi souvent que je le pourrai.

Je suis néanmoins ravie que ce soit en ces moments-là que tu l'as, quand nous sommes presque toujours à l'église — bien que tu aurais pu attendre jusqu'à jeudi, sans quoi je ne serai pas en mauvaise compagnie. La comtesse Erdédy se met à tes pieds et te dit qu'elle est de très mauvaise humeur. Je ne le suis pas moins, et je crois que je l'étais hier par pressentiment. L'Archiduc te fait dire : « Très bien, tu dois avoir honte de rester en bonne santé. » Adieu, je t'attends jusqu'à ce que j'attrape cela aussi et que je puisse vraiment le faire.

Je me console sans discontinuer, en idée — mais cela ne vaut pas un seul instant de réalité. Je ne vais plus dans tes appartements. Peut-être encore un peu. Madame d'Erdédy se met à tes pieds, et j'embrasse et t'embrasse de tout mon cœur. Je suis allée voir ma fille qui t'envoie aussi un baiser.

Bonne nuit, dors bien. Je souhaite le bonsoir à Vasquez, à la comtesse Goës et à la comtesse Wallis.
views.literal_english_old:
March 1763

I am delighted, dear Sister, that you have slept. I had no doubt that the Empress's visit would do you good. I am sorry for you for the grief [that separation causes me] — and sorry for the time I shall have to spend without seeing you. It broke my heart so much that I almost began to cry. I shall try to console myself by writing to you as often as I can.

I am nonetheless delighted that it is at such a time that you have it — when we are almost always at church — though you might still have waited until Thursday; at least I shall not be in bad company. The [Countess] Erdédy places herself at your feet and tells you that she is in a very bad temper. I am no less so, and I believe I was so yesterday by presentiment. The Archduke sends you word: "Very good — you ought to be ashamed of staying in good health." Farewell — I wait in patience until I too contract it and can truly come to you.

I console myself without ceasing — in imagination — but that is not worth a single moment of reality. I no longer go to your apartments. Perhaps yet. Madame d'Erdédy places herself at your feet, and I kiss you and kiss you with all my heart. I have been to see my daughter, who also sends you a kiss.

Good evening; sleep well. I wish good evening to [Vasquez], to [Countess] Goës, and to [Countess] Wallis.

views.plain_english:
March 1763

I'm so glad you slept, dear Sister. I knew the Empress's visit would do you good. I feel terrible about the sadness of not being able to see you — it has broken my heart so completely I almost burst into tears. I will do my best to console myself by writing to you as often as I can.

All the same, I'm glad it happened when it did, since we're almost always at church at these times anyway. You could have waited until Thursday though — at least I'd have had some decent company. Countess Erdédy sends you her regards and says she is in a foul mood. So am I — and I think I already was yesterday, as if I had a premonition. The Archduke asks me to tell you: "Well done — you should be ashamed of staying healthy." Goodbye — I'll wait until I catch it too and can actually come to you.

I comfort myself constantly in my imagination — but it is worth nothing compared to a single real moment with you. I've stopped going to your apartments. Perhaps for just a little while longer. Madame d'Erdédy sends her respects, and I kiss you and kiss you with all my heart. I went to see my little daughter, who sends you a kiss as well.

Good night — sleep well. My fond good evenings to Vasquez, Countess Goës, and Countess Wallis.

I'm going to work as much as I can until noon, then not possible because of my headache, which was very bad. But on the other hand, the Empress came to see me afterwards, I was already in bed, and when the comedy would have earned the Augustinians six high masses, I am looking forward to two walks which will be much better. Do you want to know how I'm doing? I would tell you wonderfully, of course I slept well; I only have a very small remnant of encryption which causes a little headache but very little. I am not going to the [column?], the Empress forbade me to do so. She is there at 3 o'clock. I will go to your house during this time if I have

letters.closing: I kiss you because I have to get dressed to go to the Saurau

views.original_french: Spring 1763 I hope, dear Sister, that you will have been happy with your habit; I am quite so myself. I would like to be as much at the table, that is to say, if she were already at your place. Let me tell me how your tooth is. I'm in a bad mood; have it refueled every twenty-four hours. I have seen teeth just as bad and just as sensitive become leadable and last a long time afterwards. But for that, you need to know if the gasoline has not greatly increased your pain; in this case she will come to reason. But even if you don't use gasoline, don't have it sealed before this kind of inflammation in the whole head is cleared. Farewell, I kiss you because I have to get dressed to go to the Saurau.

letters.closing: I kiss you

views.original_french: Spring 1763 I hope that your fear has disappeared or will disappear when you learn that I am doing very well, although I woke up more than forty times last night. I flatter myself that you are at least as good as the family who all agree that they cannot be 1 strs of their own doing. For me, if you want me to be right, it will be too late, and since you are already determined to burn her, you can boldly have her sealed tomorrow for having tried everything. Perhaps this will succeed; otherwise, it will be neither worse nor better, because you will suffer, I answer you. Farewell. Hello Vasquez. You make me say that I am krantig; I am right to be when I see the donkeys and the fools making deliberations which I respond as a living soul and give you tomorrow. So farewell 2 therefore the journey of Fischamend. I don't know how I didn't die when I found out, but I had a prophetic spirit when I told you that I was going to prepare myself for death. I will do it with all the more care as the pain could kill me. I would be angry because neither your table nor what I owe you when I die is not finished yet. But I might still have time to speak to you before I expire. Goodbye, I kiss you. we kissed until we were exhausted. I don't yet have the account of the signed table, I assure you it doesn't cost more.

I was even tempted to destroy what was done and that would have happened if I had not feared your wrath. By the way, and as for my sister Marie-Anne, you will never have her. Likewise, I could have taken advantage of a favorable moment with the Empress to make her have someone, but I reflected that you would no longer love Vasquez if you had her alone, which would be the greatest of misfortunes. So I judged that it was better to leave you with something to be jealous of than to risk everything. Besides, as my death is imminent, my sister Marie-Anne will resume. His character is more suited to yours than those who may resemble me if, to make matters worse, they are not ardent. So everything will be fine for then. I was even tempted to destroy what was done and that would have happened if I had not feared your wrath. By the way, and as for my sister Marie-Anne, you will never have her. Likewise, I could have taken advantage of a favorable moment with the Empress to make her have someone, but I reflected that you would no longer love Vasquez if you had her alone, which would be the greatest of misfortunes. So I judged that it was better to leave you with something to be jealous of than to risk everything. Besides, as my death is imminent, my sister Marie-Anne will resume. His character is more suited to yours than those who may resemble me if, to make matters worse, they are not ardent. So everything will be fine for then. Goodbye, sorry, my note is indecipherable but when you have a very strong bloating in your room, your hand is not very confident. In truth, the one I had at the moment is almost over. Don't at least believe that my predictions this morning are verified in that my head is spinning. I wanted to scare you but I cannot leave you worried. I'm very lazy it's true, but I still love you. Farewell once again, I kiss you and ask you to forgive me for everything I might have written. I even ask you to dispense with it forever. 1. Is this his friendly will, “Advice to Mary”? that you will know how to take a time that would not have inconvenienced you to read this post. I love you adoringly and my happiness is to love you, and to be loved by you, it is the greatest contentment I can have. My happiness depends on you, it is you who make it. You also know that I constantly persecute you, but it is because I love you. Your perfection is all I wish for, perhaps we will never see each other again, perhaps we will no longer be together; these moments were too sweet for me to be able to boast of seeing them return. You will never miss anything, as long as you have the Vasquez; she is able to tell you your truths and make you derive an advantage from the trust you have in her, your friendship for me is a superfluity which, if it is dear to your heart, is not so necessary to you. The good Lord knows what he will do. Perhaps we will be separated, perhaps death will end a life which is dear to me only because it is dedicated to you. What I can tell you is that the Empress herself is beginning to be pleased with your conduct. Towards my sister Marie-Anne, continue for even because I fear that the arrival of Salmour will cause us some small undue movement. But above all, please always refrain from judging people's thoughts, because you will often be wrong. You will make endless rash judgments, and basically, it is contrary to all of Christianity. No matter how much you preach about your devotion, it doesn't matter when your conduct does not respond to it, and if not out of love for God, then at least for me. Think about it. It's not about praying: do your homework, that's true devotion. If you get used to it, you will become master of your first movements and even for the world this is necessary. Also, never talk about anything that might make you angry, unless you are confident of your composure. And don't talk about all the ideas you have about your neighbor. Believe that it is of more consequence than you think for your soul. Cast out the thought of it as bad, because although it is only us who say it, it is still worrying about it, which is reprehensible. Sorry, but what would be the point of being loved in this world if we had to be separated for an eternity? And besides, I am perhaps an object of sin to you, a light one in truth. At least I flatter myself about it, so that I can try to repair it through my speeches. Farewell, I kiss you.

views.original_french: October-November 1763 Hello, kind, adorable, 1 dear [...] Sister, as I do not know what to become, having already played the violin and being neither eating, nor writing, nor painting, I find no other resource to give me some taste for work than to present myself at your feet in writing, being too lazy to do it in reality. You wanted to know my news this morning, but how can I hold my head, my chest, my stomach, my stomach in a ball like your ambassador? I know that I knew how to bend so as to be able to form one myself, but since twenty years ago, and I was smaller, I don't know how that would succeed. However, I would try it again if I did not fear crushing the child Jesus of 2 my famous painting, which by delaying it could well disturb my brush. So I will tell you to satisfy your curiosity, which I know is quite lively, that my head, my chest, my stomach, my stomach are doing wonderfully, but that the more worried I am about my sister Marie-Anne's cold, the more I envy her fate, although I am convinced that I will perhaps be dispatched sooner than her. You will undoubtedly scold and rail against me, poor creature who does no harm and wishes above all for your happiness. This is the moment of ideas that still occupied me despite all the efforts I made to chase them away. I cannot absolutely, and whatever I do, conceive that I must see another year pass, and if there were sure announcements of death, this should be one of them. I would take it if I believed myself holy enough for an inspiration from Heaven, because such a strong, calm presentiment is rare, I believe, to find. I can say that it seems to me that a secret voice announces it to me and this decree, which should disturb me, spreads a sweetness, an anointing in my soul that I cannot understand and even less express. She encourages me in everything and gives me strength greater than myself. For two days since this has held me, I have been in a delicious state and I do not know that all the joys that one can experience in the world can equal this sweetness, this interior satisfaction that I feel. But as I am not a saint, I believe that my head is spinning, and that as the one closest to going crazy in the whole family, it would not be fair for me to let myself be preceded by you, who also have a disposition to do so. In any case, for anything that could happen, I'm going to start the painting you want. I'll make another child in it in the meantime, because they all look the same and it will be easy to then change a few features that will make it meaningful. Farewell, dear Laurette, don't go making me seem like a visionary in everyone's minds, because your anger could make you talk. That's enough of the Vasquez to relieve her by telling her even worse what you want from me I kiss you millions of times with all my soul I need a response 3 by mouth or in writing, as well[...] . illegible. 2. Overlap of several themes in the symbolic mode: that of the child she is carrying mixes with the child she is painting. 3. An illegible word.
