content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 007 contain one of the most celebrated passages in the entire correspondence, in which Isabelle begs Marie-Christine to play her harpsichord badly — because hearing her play beautifully might kill her with pleasure.

content_encyclopedic.text: Letter 007 appears to date from early in Isabelle's time at the Viennese court, when her intimacy with Marie-Christine had already deepened beyond any conventional sisterly affection. The passage preserved in the notes — "don't use all your weapons if you don't want to see me expire with pleasure at your feet: play your concerts badly. If the harpsichord was unpleasant to me, it has become too dear to me since I heard you and it could kill me" — is among the most discussed in the correspondence. Its combination of erotic urgency, musical specificity, and theatrical hyperbole is characteristic of Isabelle's epistolary style at its most assured.

The musical context of this passage is essential. Both Isabelle and Marie-Christine were accomplished musicians. Isabelle played the violin and harpsichord at a level Maria Theresa publicly praised; she had studied harpsichord under the court composer Wagenseil (Georg Christoph Wagenseil, 1715–1777, a leading Viennese keyboard composer who had taught Maria Theresa's children). The letter discusses the comparative difficulty of the harpsichord and bowed strings, noting the problem of bow-jumps in keyboard transcriptions and warning Wagenseil not to be told something — a detail that implies the two women were engaged in shared musical study that they preferred to keep at some distance from official supervision.

The social figures identified in the letter's notes — Countess Maria Anna von Vasquez ("Koko"), Marie-Christine's first lady-in-waiting, and Countess Héléne Isabelle Salmour, first lady to Archduchess Marie-Anne — place the letter within the specific social world of the Habsburg court. Koko appears throughout the correspondence as a trusted friend and occasional courier for notes between the two women; her presence in both households gave her a practical usefulness that Isabelle recognized and cultivated. The "friendly visit" the letter closes by mentioning — reassuring Marie-Christine that the inquiry she wanted to make concerned only a visit, not what she feared — hints at the cautious code the two women had developed for discussing their relationship.

content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 010 identify two of Maria Theresa's younger daughters — Archduchesses Marie-Jeanne-Gabrielle and Marie-Josephe — both of whom died young, framing the smallpox catastrophe that would eventually claim Isabelle herself.

content_encyclopedic.text: Archduchess Marie-Jeanne-Gabrielle of Austria (November 4, 1750 – December 23, 1762) was the fourteenth of Maria Theresa's sixteen children and one of the family's youngest daughters when Isabelle arrived in Vienna. Known at court as Jeanne, she was twelve years old and apparently healthy when letter 010 was written in 1760 or 1761. She died on December 23, 1762, of smallpox, at the age of twelve — a death that Isabelle tracked with anguish through her letters in the weeks preceding it, beginning with the ominous note in letter 105 that something about Archduchess Jeanne seemed wrong.

Archduchess Marie-Josephe of Austria (March 19, 1751 – October 15, 1767) was the fifteenth child of Maria Theresa and outlived Isabelle by nearly four years, dying at sixteen of smallpox in 1767. She had been designated by her mother for marriage to the future Louis XVI of France but died before the arrangement could be concluded; that role eventually fell to her younger sister Marie-Antoinette. The identification of these two archduchesses in the notes to letter 010 places the letter's emotional landscape within the context of a family that smallpox was slowly dismantling.

The smallpox pattern within the Habsburg family in the early 1760s must have registered with Isabelle as a private statistical horror. Archduke Charles Joseph (1745–1761) died in January 1761. Archduchess Jeanne died in December 1762. Isabelle herself contracted the disease after giving birth in November 1763 and died nine days later. Maria Theresa, who survived her own bout in 1767, subsequently became one of the earliest royal advocates of variolation; the loss she suffered in these years — three of her children and her beloved daughter-in-law — was the experiential foundation of that conviction. Van Swieten, the court physician present throughout, was deeply sceptical of inoculation, and his conservatism may have cost lives.

entries.name: Editor's notes — letter-020
entries.short: Historian's editorial annotations for this letter.

content_contextual.text: This probably concerns the date of Isabelle's birthday, December 31, 1760. She is 19 years old.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 020 identifies a probable reference to Isabelle's nineteenth birthday on December 31, 1760 — her first birthday in Vienna, spent at a court she had entered only two months earlier.

content_encyclopedic.text: Isabelle de Bourbon-Parma was born on December 31, 1741, which meant her birthday fell on New Year's Eve — a date that gave it a particular resonance in the calendar of the Habsburg court, where the transition between years was marked by religious ceremony and formal celebration. Her nineteenth birthday, on December 31, 1760, was her first in Vienna. She had arrived in October, married Archduke Joseph on October 6 at the Hofburg, and spent two months learning the rhythms and hierarchies of her new world before this date arrived.

The significance of identifying this specific birthday in the editorial apparatus is that letter 020 falls near the beginning of the correspondence's emotional intensification. By December 1760, Isabelle had known Marie-Christine for approximately two months in person, having written to her from Parma before. The tone of the letters at this period — playful, pressing, increasingly intimate — suggests that the friendship had moved rapidly from formal sisterhood to something much more personal. A birthday letter written at this juncture would carry both the conventional good wishes of court correspondence and the overloaded emotional freight of everything the two women were becoming to each other.

Isabelle's relationship to her own birthdays was shadowed by premonition. In her later letters she refers to December 31 as a date she does not expect to reach; she speaks of completing each year as a small miracle. Her actual death came on November 27, 1763 — just over a month before what would have been her twenty-second birthday — as if her premonitions had been calibrated to the wrong side of the calendar. The note in letter 020 anchors a specific birthday in a year of beginnings; the reader who knows the arc of her story encounters it as the first of only three she would celebrate in Vienna.

entries.name: Editor's notes — letter-024
entries.short: Historian's editorial annotations for this letter.

content_contextual.text: Archduke Charles Joseph [February 1, 1745 – January 18, 1761] fell ill on December 26, 1760, with smallpox. He died on January 18, 1761.

content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 024 record the illness and death of Archduke Charles Joseph, Maria Theresa's son, who contracted smallpox on December 26, 1760, and died on January 18, 1761, at the age of fifteen — the first major death Isabelle witnessed at the Habsburg court.

content_encyclopedic.text: Archduke Charles Joseph of Austria (February 1, 1745 – January 18, 1761) was the sixth child and third surviving son of Maria Theresa and Emperor Francis I. He fell ill with smallpox on December 26, 1760, just four days before Isabelle's nineteenth birthday, and the Habsburg court spent the last days of 1760 and the first weeks of 1761 watching his decline. He died on January 18, 1761, at fifteen years old. Maria Theresa's grief was profound and public. The letter 024 notes place this death in the immediate context of the correspondence: Isabelle was watching this child die at exactly the period when her relationship with Marie-Christine was deepening most rapidly.

The death of Charles Joseph was the first of three smallpox deaths Isabelle would witness in the Habsburg family — the others being Archduchess Jeanne in December 1762 and her own death in November 1763. The pattern was visible to those living through it. Isabelle's letter 107 explicitly alludes to Charles Joseph when Jeanne falls ill two years later: "Allusion to Archduke Charles, who died two years previously of the same illness." She watched the same disease take the same path twice before it took her. The horror of this is understated in the editorial notes but entirely present in the correspondence itself.

Court smallpox in the eighteenth century moved through noble households with terrifying speed. The virus spread through contaminated fabrics and close personal contact — precisely the modes of transmission that court life made unavoidable. Inoculation by variolation was known and practiced in England and parts of the Ottoman world, but the Habsburg court under Van Swieten's conservative medical direction did not adopt it. Maria Theresa eventually championed inoculation after her own bout in 1767, but by then she had lost Charles Joseph, Jeanne, Isabelle, and — to this same disease — her daughter-in-law Maria Josepha (died 1767). The deaths were preventable.

content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 026 suggest that Isabelle is quoting from a piece she wrote herself — possibly theatrical or musical — and reflect her consistent perception that her family environment carried dangers of corruption, unhappiness, or misanthropy.

content_encyclopedic.text: The passage quoted in the notes to letter 026 — describing someone who "often finds in her own family something to sadden her" and who navigates "the difference in characters, the intrigues which are all too frequent at Court" — has the cadence of a philosophical observation rather than an epistolary aside. The editor's suggestion that it comes from a theatrical or musical piece composed by Isabelle raises the question of how much of her creative work has been lost: beyond the prose treatises preserved in Parma, there are references in the correspondence to compositions — concerts, pieces she played for Marie-Christine — that have not survived.

The content of the passage is revealing regardless of its genre. Isabelle's diagnosis of the Habsburg court — "the difference in characters, the intrigues which are all too frequent at Court, put it in daily danger either of becoming perverted, or of becoming unhappy or misanthropic" — is precise and unsentimental. She is describing a systemic danger: that the court's combination of enforced proximity, hierarchical competition, and constant surveillance tends to produce in its inhabitants one of three outcomes, each worse than the last. This is the analytical voice of someone who has spent two years observing the institution with the detachment of a philosopher while being trapped within it as a participant.

The phrase "her own family" in this context is deliberately ambiguous — it could refer to the Habsburg family into which Isabelle had married, or to the Bourbon-Parma family she had left behind, or to both simultaneously. Her letters show a sophisticated awareness of family as a political structure as much as an emotional one: she writes with affection about Maria Theresa, with careful management about Joseph, with occasional warmth about her Viennese sisters-in-law, and with the measured distance of someone who has analysed each relationship and knows precisely what it will and will not bear. The family, in both courts, was never simply home.

content_contextual.text: Charlotte Sophie, Countess von Bentinck von Réne, née Countess von Aldenburg [1715-1800]. She stayed in Vienna from December 1758 to the end of September 1761. 3. “Little donkey. »

content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 054 identify Charlotte Sophie, Countess von Bentinck, a Dutch aristocrat who spent three years in Vienna from December 1758 and appears briefly in Isabelle's social world.

content_encyclopedic.text: Charlotte Sophie, Countess von Bentinck, née Countess von Aldenburg (1715–1800), was a Dutch noblewoman who became notable in mid-eighteenth-century European aristocratic circles as a traveler, correspondent, and figure of independent social ambition. Born into the Aldenburg family, she had married Count William Bentinck of Portland, grandson of the first Earl of Portland (the close confidant of William III of Orange). By the time she visited Vienna she was separated from her husband and operating with the considerable freedom that a well-connected noblewoman of independent means could achieve in this period.

Bentinck's stay in Vienna from December 1758 to the end of September 1761 overlapped with Isabelle's arrival and the first year of her life at court. She moved in the circles of the high Viennese aristocracy and would have encountered the new Archduchess early. The reference to her in letter 054 suggests she was a figure of sufficient interest or prominence in the social world the two women shared that her presence or behaviour required commentary. Bentinck was known as a letter-writer and social observer in her own right; her correspondence with figures across northern Europe is preserved in Dutch archives.

The precise nature of Bentinck's significance to letter 054 cannot be determined from the editorial note alone — whether she was a figure of admiration, amusement, or political relevance in the specific letter is unclear without reading the letter itself. Her dates in Vienna (she left at the end of September 1761) mean that she was present during the death of Archduke Charles Joseph in January 1761 and for the first intense year of Isabelle and Marie-Christine's correspondence. An independent, socially prominent woman traveling without her husband, operating in the court world with evident confidence, might well have been a figure Isabelle observed with interest.

entries.name: Editor's notes — letter-065
entries.short: Historian's editorial annotations for this letter.

content_contextual.text: Count Rodolphe de Colloredo [1706-1788] was vice-chancellor of court and state. He headed the services of the imperial chancellery in Vienna.

content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 065 identify Count Rodolphe de Colloredo, vice-chancellor of the imperial court, as a significant figure — the head of the imperial chancellery in Vienna and therefore one of the senior administrators of the Habsburg state.

content_encyclopedic.text: Count Rodolphe de Colloredo (1706–1788) served as Vice-Chancellor of Court and State under Maria Theresa, heading the services of the imperial chancellery in Vienna. The Colloredo family was one of the great noble houses of the Austrian hereditary lands — originally from Friuli, they had served the Habsburgs for generations in military, ecclesiastical, and administrative capacities. Rodolphe's position made him one of the senior figures of the bureaucratic apparatus that governed the day-to-day administration of the Habsburg state alongside the politically dominant Chancellor Kaunitz.

The appearance of Colloredo in letter 065 connects the world of Isabelle's private correspondence with the machinery of Habsburg governance. Her letters show consistent awareness of the administrative structures around her — the State Council, the chancellery, the pattern of councils that governs Joseph's schedule — and Colloredo's chancellery was the institutional centre of much of this. His daughter Marie-Gabrielle, identified in the notes to letter 089, appears later in the correspondence as a figure in the women's social world, suggesting that the Colloredo family connection was one Isabelle encountered personally as well as institutionally.

The Vice-Chancellor's role in the imperial chancellery placed him at the intersection of foreign policy, domestic administration, and court protocol. Letter 065 falls in the middle period of the correspondence, when Isabelle was fully established at court and her network of social and political observation was at its most developed. A reference to Colloredo at this period could involve anything from a diplomatic matter to a scheduling question affecting her access to Marie-Christine. The precision of the editorial identification suggests his appearance was specific enough to require explanation for a reader unfamiliar with the court hierarchy.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 074 refers to the Vienna Political Correspondence archives — the Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv — indicating that the letter or its context is corroborated or illuminated by official diplomatic records held there.

content_encyclopedic.text: The Vienna Political Correspondence referenced in the notes to letter 074 belongs to the Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv (HHStA) — the House, Court, and State Archive that was the central repository of Habsburg administrative and diplomatic records. Founded in the sixteenth century as the imperial archive and reorganized under Maria Theresa, it holds the diplomatic correspondence of the Habsburg state across several centuries, including the voluminous letters exchanged between Vienna, Versailles, Madrid, and Parma during the period of Isabelle's life.

The use of the Political Correspondence folio archives to annotate a private letter of Isabelle's is methodologically significant: it means the editor has found a point at which the intimate correspondence and the official diplomatic record intersect — a person, an event, or a political reference that appears in both Isabelle's private world and the official documentation of the Habsburg state. This is precisely the kind of double verification that makes historical annotation valuable. Letter 074 evidently refers to something sufficiently specific and politically legible to be traceable in the state archives.

Alfred von Arneth, the great nineteenth-century director of the HHStA who proposed suppressing five of Isabelle's letters, knew the Political Correspondence intimately — his Geschichte Maria Theresias drew on it extensively. The irony that his recommendation of suppression failed, and that the present edition uses the very archives he directed to annotate the letters he wished hidden, is a small but satisfying loop of archival history. The HHStA records, combined with the Budapest correspondence, now allow a fuller picture of Isabelle's world than any single archive could provide.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 081 identifies a member of the Khevenhüller family — wife or daughter of Count Jean-Joseph de Khevenhüller, the Grand Chamberlain at the Habsburg court.

content_encyclopedic.text: Count Jean-Joseph de Khevenhüller (1706–1776) served as Grand Chamberlain (Oberstkämmerer) at the Habsburg court — the senior court official responsible for the management of the imperial household and all its ceremonial functions. The position was one of the most prestigious in the court hierarchy, held exclusively by members of the highest Austrian nobility. Khevenhüller is also known to historians as the author of an extensive diary — the Aus der Zeit Maria Theresias — that provides one of the most detailed contemporary accounts of court life in the 1740s–1770s, including observations of Isabelle and her husband.

The wife or daughter of Khevenhüller who appears in letter 081 would have been a prominent figure in Isabelle's immediate social world. The Grand Chamberlain's family occupied a central position in court society; his wife would have been among the senior ladies present at imperial ceremonies and social events, while his daughters would have moved in the circles of the younger archduchesses. That she appears in a letter to Marie-Christine suggests she was a figure both women knew well enough to discuss without needing further identification — a mark of social proximity.

Khevenhüller's diary, published in the nineteenth century from his manuscript, records Isabelle's arrival at court in October 1760 and several subsequent observations of her behaviour and character. His testimony — like that of Albert of Saxe-Teschen's memoir — represents the outsider's view of a woman the correspondence allows us to see from inside. That the editor finds it necessary to identify his family member in letter 081 suggests that Isabelle's letter engages with this woman in a substantive way — as a social actor requiring explanation, not merely a name in passing.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 082 establishes that Easter in 1762 fell on April 10 — anchoring the letter within the liturgical calendar that governed the Habsburg court's annual rhythm.

content_encyclopedic.text: The calculation that Easter 1762 fell on April 10 is a standard chronological tool for dating undated letters in the correspondence. Because Isabelle rarely dated her letters, the editors have relied extensively on internal references to datable events — deaths, illnesses, court ceremonies, and the fixed dates of the liturgical calendar — to establish a plausible sequence. Easter Sunday, as a moveable feast calculated by the Gregorian calendar used across Catholic Europe, provides a precise anchor when letters mention it or refer to the period around it.

The liturgical year at the Habsburg court was observed with considerable intensity. Lent, Holy Week, Easter, and the major feasts of the Marian calendar all governed the pace of court social life: during Lent entertainments were curtailed, concerts were restricted to religious music, and attendance at devotions was expected of all court members. For Isabelle, whose relationship with Marie-Christine involved stolen meetings during the court's social events, the liturgical calendar was both a religious framework and a practical constraint. Letters written near Easter 1762 fall in a period when Archduchess Jeanne was still alive and the worst of the smallpox catastrophe was still eight months away.

April 1762 represents, in the trajectory of the correspondence, one of the last periods of relative equilibrium before the sequence of crises that marks the final year and a half of Isabelle's life. Jeanne would fall ill in late 1762, die in December, and Isabelle would begin experiencing the joint pain noted in letter 109 and the miscarriage of January 1763 before her final pregnancy and death in November 1763. A letter anchored to Easter 1762 belongs to the period when both women were still navigating court life without the immediate shadow of catastrophic loss — a shadow that would descend soon enough.

content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 089 identify the Genevan painter Jean-Étienne Liotard, who visited Vienna from April to November 1762 and made portraits of the imperial family, and Marie-Gabrielle Colloredo, daughter of the court vice-chancellor.

content_encyclopedic.text: Jean-Étienne Liotard (1702–1789) was one of the most distinctive portrait painters of the eighteenth century. Born in Geneva of French Huguenot parents, he spent extended periods at the Ottoman court in Constantinople, where he adopted Turkish dress — an affectation he maintained throughout his later career in Europe, which earned him the nickname "the Turkish painter." He worked in pastel, a medium then at the height of its European fashion, and his portraits combined meticulous technical finish with an unusually direct psychological observation. His Vienna visit in 1762 produced portraits of Maria Theresa and members of the imperial family.

Liotard's presence in Vienna from April to November 1762 coincided with a remarkable period in court life: the visit of the young Mozart in October 1762, Gluck's operatic reforms at the court opera, and the worsening health of the Habsburg family that would take Archduchess Jeanne in December. Isabelle's reference to him in letter 089 — if she is indeed referring to Liotard — places her in contact with one of the most sought-after portraitists in Europe. Whether he painted her is not known from the documentary record, but the period overlaps exactly with a known portrait of Marie-Christine in pastel that may be connected to his visit.

Marie-Gabrielle Colloredo, daughter of the Vice-Chancellor Count Rodolphe de Colloredo identified in the notes to letter 065, represents the intergenerational reach of the court's social network into Isabelle's world. As the daughter of a senior court official, she would have been present at court social events and potentially part of the informal circle around the younger archduchesses and their companions. Her appearance alongside Liotard in the same editorial note suggests that letter 089 contained both artistic and social commentary — Isabelle reporting to Marie-Christine on a court visit that brought together the celebrated foreign painter and a woman both of them knew.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 096 alerts the reader to the physical condition of this letter: it was written in pencil and is almost entirely erased, with two words remaining illegible — a reminder of the fragile material survival of the correspondence.

content_encyclopedic.text: The physical state of letter 096 — written in pencil, almost completely erased — is a document in itself. Pencil was an unusual choice for correspondence in this period; ink was standard for formal letters, though pencil might be used for quick notes or drafts. That Isabelle used pencil for this letter suggests either that she was writing in circumstances where ink was unavailable or inconvenient — perhaps at a distance from her writing table, in a hurried moment, in a dark room — or that she intended the letter to be more ephemeral than her ink letters, easier to destroy. She frequently asked Marie-Christine to burn her letters; this one was perhaps its own half-destruction.

The near-total erasure of the text raises a question the editorial notes cannot resolve: was the pencil letter erased naturally over time, through handling and damp, or was it deliberately rubbed out at some point — by Marie-Christine herself, by Albert preserving what he thought appropriate, or by Arneth or another nineteenth-century archivist? The 1875 Arneth note recommending suppression of five letters demonstrates that archival censorship was contemplated; whether it extended to physical erasure, or whether nature accomplished what human caution might otherwise have done, cannot be determined.

The two illegible words noted in the annotation fall within a letter otherwise described as nearly completely erased — which means the surviving text itself must be fragmentary. The editor's decision to include the letter in the edition despite its physical state is a scholarly commitment: even a fragmentary, near-erased letter carries something of Isabelle's presence, some trace of the circumstances in which she wrote it, some indication of when in the sequence of their relationship it falls. The gap in the text is itself historical evidence: it tells us that something was written, and that time, accident, or intention ensured we cannot read it.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 105 tentatively identifies the beginning of Archduchess Jeanne's smallpox illness — the disease that would kill her in December 1762 — in Isabelle's observation that something seemed wrong with the young archduchess.

content_encyclopedic.text: Archduchess Marie-Jeanne-Gabrielle (November 4, 1750 – December 23, 1762) — known at court as Jeanne — appears in Isabelle's later letters as an object of anxious attention. The editor's tentative identification of letter 105 as marking the beginning of her smallpox illness places it in late 1762, a matter of weeks before her death on December 23. Isabelle had watched Archduke Charles Joseph die of the same disease in January 1761; she knew exactly what the progression looked like. The word "perhaps" in the editorial note reflects the uncertainty inherent in dating undated letters, but the emotional trajectory of the correspondence strongly supports this identification.

Letter 107 makes explicit what letter 105 only implies: "Allusion to Archduke Charles, who died two years previously of the same illness." Isabelle watching Jeanne's smallpox through the lens of Charles Joseph's death two years earlier is a document of accumulating grief. By 1762 she had been at the Habsburg court for two years; she had formed deep attachments to the younger archduchesses; and she had personal experience of what it meant to watch a teenager die of this specific disease in this specific court. The clinical distance of the editorial note — "perhaps the beginning of the illness" — cannot fully absorb the emotional weight the letters themselves carry.

The sequence of letters around Jeanne's illness and death represents one of the most harrowing sections of the correspondence. Isabelle writes to Marie-Christine about her own helplessness, her terror, her grief. The shared watching of a dying child — performed under the eyes of a court in which strong public emotion required ceremonial management — bonds the two women in a new way: they become witnesses together to a loss the court's formal machinery could not contain. When Jeanne died on December 23, 1762, Isabelle had approximately eleven months left to live. She did not know this; but the reader does.

content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 107 make explicit Isabelle's allusion to Charles Joseph's earlier death from smallpox, and identify the court physician Gérard Van Swieten — the most eminent doctor in the Habsburg world — as he attends to Archduchess Jeanne's final illness.

content_encyclopedic.text: Gérard Van Swieten (1700–1772) was the personal physician of Empress Maria Theresa and the most powerful medical figure in the Habsburg world. Born in Leiden, he had been the favourite student of the great Dutch clinician Herman Boerhaave (1668–1738), whose lectures at Leiden were attended by students from across Europe and whose influence on eighteenth-century medicine was profound. Van Swieten came to Vienna in 1745 at Maria Theresa's invitation, becoming her court physician and effectively the director of medical education and practice in the Austrian lands. He reorganized the medical faculty of Vienna University, established the first imperial library catalogue, and fought successfully against the persecution of supposed vampires in Moravia.

Van Swieten's presence at Archduchess Jeanne's bedside was the ultimate court medical resource deployed: there was no better physician in the Habsburg world. That she died anyway reflects the limits of eighteenth-century medicine against smallpox. Van Swieten, despite his Boerhaavian training in careful clinical observation, was deeply conservative on the question of inoculation: he believed the risks of variolation outweighed its benefits, a position that placed him in direct opposition to the emerging European consensus represented by figures like Lady Mary Wortley Montagu in England and the practice widely adopted after 1750 in the Ottoman world. His conservatism cost the Habsburg family dearly.

The allusion to Archduke Charles Joseph noted by the editor — "who died two years previously of the same illness" — is among the most quietly devastating moments in the editorial apparatus. Isabelle, writing to Marie-Christine about Jeanne's illness, does not need to explain the reference: they both know. They both watched Charles Joseph die in January 1761. Now it is December 1762 and the same pattern is repeating itself with a different child. The parallelism was not abstract for Isabelle: she had contracted smallpox herself before giving birth to her daughter in November 1763, and she died nine days after the birth. Van Swieten attended her too.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 109 marks the start of Isabelle's own joint pain — the first physical symptom that led, through pregnancy and smallpox, to her death in November 1763.

content_encyclopedic.text: The note "Start of Isabelle's joint pain" at letter 109 is among the most freighted annotations in the edition. Joint pain — likely inflammatory arthritis — began for Isabelle at some point in 1762 or 1763, and the editor's placement of its onset at letter 109 gives the reader a specific coordinate in the correspondence where Isabelle's body begins to fail her visibly. She would have a miscarriage in January 1763 (referenced in letter 122), survive that, and then become pregnant again — the pregnancy that ended with the birth of a daughter on November 18, 1763, and Isabelle's death nine days later on November 27.

The joint pain Isabelle describes was likely rheumatic in origin, possibly a consequence of the physical strain of her first pregnancy (she had given birth to her daughter Marie-Therese on March 20, 1762) or of the emotional stress of the period. In the eighteenth century, joint pain was treated with a range of remedies — thermal baths, rest, poultices — none of which addressed the underlying inflammation. Court medicine under Van Swieten was sophisticated by the standards of the age but still entirely pre-germ theory; the connection between infectious illness and joint inflammation was not understood.

The trajectory from this note — joint pain beginning at letter 109 — to Isabelle's death thirteen months later is one the reader follows with a kind of retrospective horror. Isabelle does not know, when she mentions her pain in this letter, that she is beginning the physical decline that will kill her. She continues to write to Marie-Christine with her characteristic combination of wit, tenderness, and philosophical lucidity. The body is deteriorating; the mind and the relationship remain vivid. The contrast between these two registers — physical decay and emotional intensity — is the central dramatic tension of the correspondence's final arc.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 122 tentatively connects it to Isabelle's miscarriage in January 1763 — a medical crisis that followed Archduchess Jeanne's death in December 1762 and preceded her final, fatal pregnancy.

content_encyclopedic.text: Isabelle's miscarriage in January 1763 came in the immediate aftermath of one of the most concentrated periods of grief the correspondence records. Archduchess Jeanne had died on December 23, 1762; Isabelle had been emotionally devastated and physically exhausted by weeks of watching the child's decline. The miscarriage that followed, placed tentatively by the editor after letter 122, may have been precipitated by this combination of grief and exhaustion. First-trimester pregnancy loss in the eighteenth century was common across all social classes and was typically understood as a providential event rather than a medical failure, but its physical and emotional consequences were no less real.

The editorial uncertainty expressed in the note's phrasing — "After her miscarriage in January 1763?" — reflects the general problem of the undated correspondence. The miscarriage is referenced in other sources, and its placement at letter 122 is based on internal evidence of tone and circumstance rather than any explicit statement by Isabelle. She was not, in general, direct in the letters about her own medical condition; she tends to understate her physical state while conveying its emotional cost obliquely. A letter written in the weeks after a miscarriage might be tonally different from one written before it, but identifying that difference from the text alone requires interpretive judgment.

The miscarriage of January 1763 was not Isabelle's first pregnancy loss, and she had already given birth to her daughter Marie-Therese on March 20, 1762. Her reproductive history — at least one miscarriage, one surviving child born in 1762, and the fatal pregnancy of 1763 — was not unusual for a young aristocratic woman of the period, but its concentration in three years of deteriorating health suggests a body under significant stress. The daughter born in November 1763 survived only until 1770, dying at seven. Isabelle's maternal line, like her own life, was cut short.

entries.name: Editor's notes — letter-138
entries.short: Historian's editorial annotations for this letter.

content_contextual.text: Vienna Political Correspondence, vol. 294, f. 100 v., March 26, 1763: “Archduchess Marie [Christine], second daughter of the Empress, with measles declared two days ago. »
Countess Rosa Wallis, lady-in-waiting to Archduchess Jeanne who served in the service of Marie-Christine.

content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 138 record that Marie-Christine had contracted measles two days before the letter was written — and identify Countess Rosa Wallis, her lady-in-waiting, who appears in the correspondence.

content_encyclopedic.text: The measles attack identified in letter 138 as having declared itself two days before Isabelle wrote places this letter in March 1763. Marie-Christine was ill; Isabelle was writing to her. In a world where measles could be dangerous — it was less lethal than smallpox but still a serious febrile illness capable of producing complications — a bout of measles in a young woman with whom one had an intimate relationship was a source of genuine anxiety. Isabelle's response would have been conditioned by everything she had already witnessed: Charles Joseph dead of smallpox, Jeanne dead of smallpox, her own body beginning to decline.

The note dates this letter to March 1763, placing it approximately four months before the summer that would bring Isabelle's final pregnancy and eight months before her death. At this point in the correspondence Isabelle is simultaneously managing her own physical deterioration — joint pain, aftermath of miscarriage — and watching those she loves fall ill around her. The emotional texture of letters from this period is, by all accounts, one of concentrated tenderness: she writes to Marie-Christine from a place that knows it is temporary, that the relationship itself is living on borrowed time.

Countess Rosa Wallis, identified as Marie-Christine's lady-in-waiting, was part of the intimate domestic world around the archduchess that formed the immediate social environment of the two women's relationship. Ladies-in-waiting served as practical intermediaries, guardians of private time, and confidantes of varying degrees of trust. The fact that Rosa Wallis is named in the notes — rather than simply referred to as "a lady-in-waiting" — suggests she was a sufficiently specific and known figure in the correspondence to require identification for the reader. Her nationality, family background, and relationship with Marie-Christine are not established by the editorial note alone.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 146 establishes that Easter Sunday in 1763 fell on April 3 — a chronological anchor placing this letter in the spring of the last year of Isabelle's life.

content_encyclopedic.text: The calculation that Easter 1763 fell on April 3 provides a precise chronological anchor for letter 146. Easter 1763 falls approximately seven months before Isabelle's death on November 27 of the same year. A letter written around this date belongs to the final act of the correspondence: Isabelle's joint pain is established, her miscarriage of January has been survived, Marie-Christine's measles (letter 138, March 1763) are presumably over, and the summer that will bring Isabelle's final pregnancy is still some months away. April 3, 1763 is a moment of apparent calm between recent illness and impending catastrophe.

Easter at the Habsburg court was observed with great ceremonial intensity. Holy Week required attendance at specific religious services each day; Easter Sunday was marked by a public ceremony in which the emperor and empress demonstrated humility by washing the feet of twelve poor people — the Maundy ceremony, performed since the medieval period as an act of Christian charity. The court that had been subdued through Lent came back to life at Easter with renewed social activity. For Isabelle and Marie-Christine, the return of social gatherings after Lenten restriction meant renewed opportunities for the meetings and concerts that form the physical substrate of their relationship.

The precision of the editorial dating — establishing Easter 1763 as April 3 — reflects the larger project of reconstructing a chronological sequence from an undated correspondence. The editors have worked backwards and forwards from fixed points: deaths, known court events, the dates of specific ceremonies. Easter Sunday, being fixed each year by the Gregorian ecclesiastical calendar, is one of the most reliable such anchors. The result is a correspondence that, while undated in the manuscripts, can be placed with reasonable confidence within a sequence of historical time — allowing the reader to experience not just the emotional arc of Isabelle's letters but their place in the calendar of events leading to her death.

content_contextual.text: Countess Marie-Christine von Thun [1738-1788].

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 153 identifies Countess Marie-Christine von Thun (1738–1788) — a member of the prominent Bohemian noble family who appears in the social world of the correspondence.

content_encyclopedic.text: Countess Marie-Christine von Thun (1738–1788) belonged to the House of Thun-Hohenstein, one of the oldest and most distinguished noble families of Bohemia, with extensive estates and a long history of service to the Habsburg dynasty. The Thun family provided ministers, bishops, and court officials across several generations; their prominence in Vienna was matched by their roots in the Bohemian nobility that formed one of the pillars of Habsburg aristocratic culture. A Thun countess of the right generation and rank would have been a natural figure in the Viennese court world of the 1760s.

Marie-Christine von Thun's dates (1738–1788) place her as five years older than Isabelle and four years older than Marie-Christine of Austria. She would have been an established figure at court when Isabelle arrived — someone who already knew the architecture of the social world that Isabelle was entering. Whether she appears in letter 153 as a friend, a social acquaintance, a figure of court intrigue, or simply someone whose behaviour or circumstances required reporting to Marie-Christine cannot be determined from the editorial note alone.

The shared name — Marie-Christine von Thun, Marie-Christine of Austria — was not unusual in a Catholic aristocratic world where a limited number of names circulated through naming practices tied to patron saints and family tradition. Its coincidence here may have caused social comedy or confusion in the court world; Isabelle, with her characteristic eye for the telling detail, may well have noted it. Letter 153 falls in the summer of 1763, within the final months of Isabelle's life, when the correspondence takes on an increasing quality of presence and urgency — each letter a gift of time to someone both women may have suspected was running out of it.

content_brief.text: The editor's note to letter 174 identifies the subject of Isabelle's comment as Archduchess Marie-Anne — Maria Theresa's eldest daughter, known within the family as the 'erudite' one for her interest in science and learning.

content_encyclopedic.text: Archduchess Marie-Anne of Austria (September 6, 1738 – November 19, 1789) was the eldest surviving daughter of Maria Theresa and Emperor Francis I. Born before the political crises that dominated her parents' early reign, she was a woman of genuine intellectual interests — the sciences in particular — in a court that valued music and piety above learning of the naturalist kind. She never married; Maria Theresa offered various explanations including poor health, but Marie-Anne's determination to remain unmarried and pursue her scholarly interests was an open secret at court.

Marie-Anne's reputation as the family's "erudite" member gave her a particular position in the court's social typology: she was the exception, the one daughter whose life was defined by intellectual rather than matrimonial achievement. For Isabelle, who was herself a philosopher and writer of unusual depth, Marie-Anne would have been an interesting figure — simultaneously a kindred spirit and a cautionary example of what a life organized around the mind rather than marriage looked like within the Habsburg system. Isabelle's comment in letter 174 might be admiring, affectionate, amused, or some combination of all three.

The appearance of Marie-Anne in letter 174, which falls in the later part of the correspondence, situates Isabelle still within the social world of the court even as her health declined. She continued to observe, report, and comment on the personalities around her with the precision that characterizes the entire correspondence. Marie-Anne — who would outlive Isabelle by twenty-six years, remaining at the Vienna court until her death in 1789 as a fixture of the imperial household — represents a kind of life Isabelle never had the time to either embrace or reject: the long, scholarly, unmarried existence of a woman whose mind outlasted her dynastic usefulness.

content_brief.text: The editor's notes to letter 182 reference court politics and Isabelle's declining health — placing this letter among the last of the correspondence, written in the autumn of 1763 as her body was failing and her death was weeks or months away.

content_encyclopedic.text: Letter 182 falls near the end of the surviving correspondence, which terminates with Isabelle's death on November 27, 1763. By the autumn of that year, Isabelle's health was in serious decline: her joint pain had been established since at least late 1762, she had survived a miscarriage in January 1763, and she was now in the final weeks of another pregnancy. She gave birth to a daughter on November 18, 1763; she contracted smallpox — whether during the birth or in the days immediately following — and died nine days later. The daughter, named Maria Christina after Marie-Christine of Austria, survived her mother by less than a year.

The court politics referenced in the note to letter 182 are not specified in detail, but they belong to the political world of late 1763: the end of the Seven Years' War (February 1763, Treaty of Hubertusburg), the consolidation of Maria Theresa's reformed administration under Kaunitz, and the ongoing management of the imperial family's dynastic strategy. Archduke Joseph, now a widower, would remarry in 1765 (to Maria Josepha of Bavaria); the political calculations around his second marriage were already being made in the autumn of 1763. Isabelle, whose advice to Marie-Christine had included careful guidance on how to navigate the court after her death, may have been observing these maneuvers with the detached interest of someone who knows she will not be present for their conclusion.

The emotional register of the correspondence's final letters is described by those who have read them in the original French as extraordinary: concentrated, present, intensely alive to the fact of Isabelle's own impermanence. She does not write as someone preparing a literary farewell — the letters remain practical, warm, and occasionally playful — but they have the quality of someone who has internalized the possibility of sudden ending. Albert of Saxe-Teschen, writing of her long after her death, noted that her face always showed "a tendency to dark ideas which proved that she was not perfectly happy" — and that despite this, or perhaps because of it, she possessed a quality of presence that made those around her feel they were in contact with something rare and irreplaceable. The letters to Marie-Christine are that presence, preserved.

gap_scenes.title: The Letter Unfolded Again
gap_scenes.text:
She read it a third time before the candle guttered.

The letter had arrived at Colorno in the afternoon, carried upstairs by a footman who could not have known what he held — a folded sheet from Vienna, from a woman Isabelle had never met, written in French with a lightness that made the words seem almost careless. Almost. Isabelle had pressed the paper flat against her writing table and traced the signature with one finger: Marie-Christine.

Now the July evening lay warm and close around her. The windows stood open to the park, and the smell of cut grass came in with the insects. Isabelle put the letter down and looked at the dark ceiling.

She had written back, she knew, too eagerly. She had told Marie-Christine that her feelings were too strong for eloquence, and this was true and also embarrassing — she was nineteen, she was about to be transported like goods to a court she had never seen, to marry a man she had never met, and the only person who had written to her from that place was a princess she did not know, and already Isabelle loved her.

She picked up the letter again. The victory over the Prussians was in there too, General Laudon, the news that had made her beside herself with joy. She was a good Austrian, she had said. She would be. It was simply the truth.

But the other thing — the line about showing her the joy of being able to tell her things — that was not about Prussians at all. That was something else.

She folded the letter, creased it precisely, and set it inside her prayer book, which was the only private place she had.

gap_scenes.title: Counting the Germans in Parma
gap_scenes.text:
By August, they were arriving in small numbers — aides, chamberlains, an Austrian lady-in-waiting with broad shoulders and a Viennese accent — and Isabelle stood at the upstairs window of the Palazzo del Giardino and watched them cross the courtyard below as though they were birds of a migrating flock that had come for her.

Five more weeks. She had written it to Marie-Christine and the number hung in the air of every room.

She tried to imagine what the woman looked like. From the letters she knew the handwriting — urgent, curving slightly to the right — and she knew the tone: generous, a little teasing, warm in a way that pressed close against the formal address. She knew that Marie-Christine played the harpsichord, and that she had written about victories, and that she thought Isabelle's qualities did not deserve such feeling as she'd offered.

On this last point Isabelle disagreed violently and in silence.

She had been drawing in the afternoons to pass the time. Bad portraits, mostly, of people she could not quite remember. She thought perhaps she was trying to draw faces she had not yet seen. She crumpled one attempt and threw it toward the basket and missed.

Her maid came in to say that two more German gentlemen had arrived below.

Isabelle pressed her forehead against the warm glass of the window. Five weeks. The summer smelled of thyme and dust, of the dry Italian earth that had been her home for all her years, and she was leaving it, and she was not sad. She was something she had no word for yet.

gap_scenes.title: First Sight at Schönbrunn
gap_scenes.text:
The ceremony lasted two hours and Isabelle did not see her clearly until it was nearly over.

There had been the procession, the presentations, the Empress watching everything with that particular attention that felt like being measured for a cabinet. There had been Joseph, her husband, standing beside her with a careful courtesy that she was already learning to read as neither warmth nor coldness but simply the way he held himself in public. There had been dozens of faces, all turned toward her, all performing welcome.

And then, at the edge of the room, near the tall windows that looked out over the formal garden, Marie-Christine.

She was not what Isabelle had constructed from the letters. She was more immediate than that — shorter, with an expression that moved quickly across her face, watching Isabelle across all the intervening silk and ceremony with something that was entirely unguarded. When their eyes met, Marie-Christine smiled. Not the court smile, which Isabelle was already learning to recognize as a kind of mask. The other kind.

Isabelle felt the recognition strike her somewhere below the ribs.

Later, when the presentations had concluded and the groups had rearranged into smaller conversations, they were brought together formally, and Marie-Christine took both her hands and said something quick and warm and a little wry about the journey from Parma, and Isabelle laughed — a real laugh, surprised out of her — and thought: so this is the voice behind the letters.

She had been in Vienna for less than a day and she already knew that the next years would be organized around a single gravitational point.

gap_scenes.title: The Harpsichord Lesson
gap_scenes.text:
The room was too warm for October and the harpsichord stood near the window with the lid raised, and Marie-Christine sat at the bench with her back to the door, playing a passage over and over that she could not quite resolve to her satisfaction.

Isabelle had been standing in the doorway for a full minute before Marie-Christine noticed her.

She stopped playing. She did not turn around immediately. There was a pause — the kind that holds more information than words — and then she turned, and her expression was the one that Isabelle was beginning to catalogue: the one that looked a little embarrassed to be caught in something genuine.

"You heard that," Marie-Christine said.

"I heard all of it," Isabelle said. She came further into the room and stood beside the harpsichord, looking at the keys. "You were doing this part —" she indicated a cluster of notes "— differently each time."

"I know which part."

"It was lovely each time."

Marie-Christine gave her a look that contained several things at once, and Isabelle met it without flinching. This was something she was also learning: how to hold Marie-Christine's gaze. It required a particular courage, not because the gaze was unkind, but because it was so entirely direct.

"I'll let you see the music," Marie-Christine said, "when it's ready."

"I'll hold you to that," Isabelle said, and sat down beside her on the bench without being invited, and after a moment Marie-Christine began to play again, and neither of them moved apart.

gap_scenes.title: Saint-Etienne
gap_scenes.text:
There was always somewhere to be.

Isabelle had understood this about court life within the first week — that one was always already late for something, always just completing something else, always visible in the process of arriving or departing. Privacy was not an absence; it was a skill, practiced in doorways and in the intervals between obligations.

On the day she had to go to Saint-Etienne, she had spent the whole morning aware that Marie-Christine was somewhere in the other wing of the palace. Not near. Not reachable by any ordinary means. It was a peculiar kind of ache, knowing the precise direction of someone and being unable to move toward them.

The carriage rattled over cobblestones. Isabelle sat very straight and looked out the window at the November streets of Vienna, the early dark already collecting in the alleyways, the breath of horses visible in the cold air. She was thinking about a different morning, one she had not had, one in which there had been no Saint-Etienne and no obligation and she had simply gone upstairs.

She thought: this is already a pattern. The wanting and the going somewhere else. The letter she would write afterward describing only the absence, not the wanting.

She was in a mood like a dog. She recognized this about herself without approval.

By the time she returned it was dark, and the palace windows were lit from within, and she thought she could see, on the upper floor, the room where Marie-Christine would be, and she went upstairs as quickly as dignity allowed.

gap_scenes.title: Court Mechanics
gap_scenes.text:
There was a version of court life that was machinery, and a version that was theater, and sometimes Isabelle could not tell them apart.

The Archduke — her husband — moved through both with a kind of mechanical precision she had come to find almost soothing in its predictability. He was not unkind. He was not particularly present. This was the arrangement, and Isabelle had understood it very quickly, and had filed it away without resentment.

What occupied her more was the question of what Marie-Christine had said to him, or he to her, or what had passed between them on some afternoon she had not witnessed. Marie-Christine had an influence over him that she wielded lightly and rarely — Isabelle had seen it once or twice, a word placed at the right moment, a redirection so smooth it barely registered. She had been impressed and also unsettled, not by the power itself but by how little Marie-Christine seemed to value it.

"If he knew everything he owes you," Isabelle wanted to say, and did not say, because there were always people nearby.

Instead she watched. She was good at watching. In Italy she had developed a whole inner life built on observation, and Vienna was simply a richer subject.

She watched Marie-Christine move across the reception room, exchanging words, touching an arm here, laughing there, and felt the familiar compression in her chest that she had not found a name for yet, or rather had named, and then decided the name was too large to be safe.

gap_scenes.title: St. Nicholas Eve
gap_scenes.text:
The Feast of St. Nicholas fell on a December evening when the palace smelled of beeswax and fir branches brought in from somewhere cold and far.

Isabelle had her own small suite of rooms by then, and she had begun to know which footsteps outside her door meant what. She knew the Empress's ladies by sound. She knew the particular quiet that meant Marie-Christine was passing in the corridor rather than approaching.

On St. Nicholas Eve, the Empress Maria Theresa sent Isabelle a small gift — a token, formal but warm — and wrote to thank her for something, though Isabelle was not entirely certain for what. She sat with the Empress's note for a long time, feeling the slight unreality of being thanked by the woman who had summoned her from Parma like a piece of necessary furniture, and who had turned out to be something far more complicated.

She wrote to Marie-Christine: please tell me if you admitted to Her Majesty that I was informed of your treason.

"Treason" was their word for small conspiracies of the friendly kind. It made Isabelle smile even writing it. It was the kind of word that only worked between two people who trusted each other with the irony — who understood that the mock-severity was a form of intimacy, not a form of accusation.

She sealed the letter and looked at the guttering candle for a long time before she called the footman.

Outside, the first snow of the season had begun, and Vienna was going white and quiet, and she was nineteen, and she was in the right place.

gap_scenes.title: The Curling Animals
gap_scenes.text:
There was a whole taxonomy of minor irritations that Marie-Christine could produce, and among them — Isabelle had discovered — the worst was the business with the heated tongs.

It was not the curling itself. Isabelle could tolerate a great deal in the service of appearance. It was the way Marie-Christine stood over the operation with an air of proprietorial interest in the outcome, as though Isabelle's hair were something she had a stake in, which she probably did, and this was exactly what was intolerable about it.

"You are," Isabelle said, sitting very still while the maid worked and Marie-Christine watched from the chair by the window, "the most unbearable creature in this palace."

Marie-Christine looked pleased with this assessment. "That seems unlikely, given the competition."

"In matters of hair. Specifically."

"I only want it to look right."

"It is already right."

"It will be more right."

Isabelle met her eyes in the mirror and held the gaze for a moment longer than was strictly necessary, and then looked away because looking away was sometimes the only way to prevent something else from happening in a room with another person present.

The maid finished. Marie-Christine came to look and tilted her head with the expression of someone who has won, and said nothing, which was the most maddening possible response.

Isabelle thought: I would write her a letter about this. I would say, with all possible gentleness, that she is unbearable. She would find it funny. I would mean it, and also not mean it at all.

gap_scenes.title: Grace and Gratitude
gap_scenes.text:
She had woken at six to a body that was not entirely her own.

This was the new condition — the nausea that arrived before full consciousness, the heaviness in the chest, the way her body seemed to be reorganizing itself around an agenda she had not set. She had sat up carefully and waited for the worst of it to pass, and then written to the Empress to thank her for a grace she had been granted — some arrangement, some permission, some small adjustment to the machinery of duty that Maria Theresa had quietly managed on her behalf.

Gratitude was one of the currencies of this world. Isabelle had grown up understanding this, and she was good at it — not false gratitude, which she found intolerable to produce, but genuine acknowledgment of kindness received. The Empress had been kinder than she'd expected. It complicated things.

She had slept a little better the previous night. This also complicated things, because she had been almost used to lying awake and using the time to think about Marie-Christine.

It was a habit she could not seem to break, and was not certain she wanted to. In the dark at three in the morning, with the whole palace sleeping around her and Joseph breathing quietly in the adjacent room, she would think about the afternoon she had spent in Marie-Christine's apartment, the way the light fell across the table, the particular sound of her laugh when something surprised her.

She finished the letter to the Empress and tried to go back to sleep and could not, and lay looking at the ceiling instead, which was at least familiar.

gap_scenes.title: The Pearl Necklace
gap_scenes.text:
There were eighteen days left until her birthday.

Isabelle was not accustomed to counting down to her own birthday. It had never seemed worth the trouble. But this year was different — she was turning nineteen on December thirty-first, and the thirty-first of December was also the last night of a year that had contained everything, and Marie-Christine had mentioned something yesterday about the pearls, and about dinner, and about wishing to speak to her, and Isabelle had said yes to all of it without knowing precisely what she was agreeing to.

The pearls were in a small box that lived in the top drawer of her writing table. She opened the drawer now and looked at them without taking them out. They were nothing extraordinary — a shorter strand, pale gray-white, the sort of thing one lent to a sister for an occasion and then received back later, or perhaps did not receive back, and this too was a kind of intimacy.

She closed the drawer.

She thought about the conversation Marie-Christine had promised her. She thought about all the things that could be said in a conversation that could not be said in a letter, or in a corridor, or in a room with three ladies and a footman and the Empress's portrait watching from the wall.

The December light was failing by half past three. Isabelle lit the candle herself, without calling anyone, and sat in the small brightness of it and thought about the new year coming, and the girl she would be on the other side of it.

gap_scenes.title: The Last Hour of the Year
gap_scenes.text:
At midnight the bells of Vienna rang and Isabelle stood at the window of her apartment and listened.

She had turned nineteen at some point earlier in the day — the birthday was officially December thirty-first and the palace had acknowledged it with the correct formalities — and now the year was ending, and she felt the precise quality of strangeness that came from being at a threshold, looking in both directions at once.

She had seen Marie-Christine at dinner. They had sat too far apart for anything but the ordinary exchange of glances across a table, which was its own form of conversation, one she had grown fluent in over these past months. A look that said: I see you. A look that said: I know what you are thinking. A look that said: there is too much silk between us and I am choosing not to think about that.

Now the dining room was empty and the candles were being extinguished by invisible hands all through the palace, and the bells were ringing, and Marie-Christine was somewhere in the east wing, and she was nineteen years old as of today, and she had been in Vienna for three months, and everything had changed.

She pressed her fingers against the cold glass of the window. Outside, Vienna was alive with sound — people in the streets, carriages, the celebratory noise of the city welcoming something new.

She thought: I will write to her tomorrow. Good evening, good new year, I love you. She already knew these words too well, already knew they were insufficient. She would send them anyway.

gap_scenes.title: The First Cough
gap_scenes.text:
It began with a cough.

Isabelle was in her own apartment when she heard — a page had come with a message, and in the message was the information that the Archduke Charles Joseph had taken to his bed three days earlier with a fever, and that the fever was being attended to, and that there was no cause for alarm.

There was always cause for alarm when they said there was no cause for alarm.

She knew what smallpox did. She had grown up knowing it, had seen it in Italy, had heard the accounting of it from her father in the dry tone that people used when cataloguing losses that had already happened. She had been in Vienna long enough to see how much of this family's life was organized around grief and its anticipation.

She found Marie-Christine in the afternoon in the state drawing room, in conversation with Countess Vasquez, and she caught her eye and held it, and in the look that passed between them was the knowledge that they were both afraid of the same thing and could not say so in this room.

Later, alone for a few minutes in the corridor outside the gallery, Isabelle took Marie-Christine's hand without thinking about it — took it and held it, briefly, the pressure of palm against palm — and said nothing, and after a moment let go.

"I will tell you when I know more," Marie-Christine said quietly.

"I know you will," Isabelle said. "Go."

Marie-Christine went. Isabelle stood in the corridor and breathed slowly and wrote the first letter in her head before she had reached her own apartment.

gap_scenes.title: Night Watch
gap_scenes.text:
The palace had a different quality at two in the morning.

Isabelle had not been sleeping — had not been trying to sleep — and was sitting at her window wrapped in a shawl when she heard the soft footstep in the corridor that she recognized as belonging to Marie-Christine's particular way of moving at speed without appearing to hurry.

She went to her door.

Marie-Christine was still dressed, which meant she had not been to bed. Her face had the specific brightness of someone sustained by worry past all ordinary exhaustion, the eyes too alert, the color in her cheeks too high.

"He had a better night," she said, before Isabelle could speak. "The previous one was — it should have been worse than it was. But this one was better."

Isabelle stepped aside from the door. Marie-Christine came in and stood in the middle of the room and looked at the portraits on the wall with the unseeing gaze of someone whose mind is elsewhere. Isabelle brought two chairs close together near the window and sat down in one, and after a moment Marie-Christine sat down in the other.

They did not speak for a while. Outside, the city was dark and silent, and the sky had the particular thickness of a January night when snow might come.

"I'm making two portraits," Isabelle said finally. "Would you like one?"

Marie-Christine looked at her sideways. "Of whom?"

"You," Isabelle said. "From memory. I'll send you the better one when it's finished."

Marie-Christine put her face in her hands for a moment, not from grief but from something more complicated. Then she straightened and said: "Make it flattering."

"I can only make it true," Isabelle said, which was not quite an answer.

gap_scenes.title: After Charles
gap_scenes.text:
Archduke Charles Joseph died on January the eighteenth.

Isabelle had been in the room three corridors away when it happened, sitting with her hands folded in her lap and her face arranged into an expression that was supposed to convey composure, while internally she was conducting a conversation with God that was more in the nature of a negotiation. She had lost the negotiation.

The palace changed after. It changed in the way that palaces change after deaths — not dramatically, but in the molecular structure of it, the way people moved through rooms differently, spoke differently, assembled their faces differently. The Empress's grief was a fact of the building now, present in the walls.

Isabelle thought about death. She wrote to Marie-Christine about it — or tried to, writing several drafts and keeping none of them, because the thing she wanted to say was that death felt like a separation, and what she was most afraid of separating from was standing at the end of the corridor every morning looking at her over the heads of ladies-in-waiting.

She sent a note about an almanac instead. She sent it with a page who she knew was discreet.

The almanac was beautiful — she had annotated it with a private code she trusted Marie-Christine to read. Look for yourself in the print that represents marriage. I could not find you there. The absence in the picture felt like a kind of abandonment by the artist, and she wanted Marie-Christine to know that she had looked, specifically, with attention, and missed finding her.

The response came back within the hour. She read it standing in the corridor and did not wait to be somewhere private, which was unlike her, and also precisely appropriate.

gap_scenes.title: The Interval of Grief
gap_scenes.text:
There were three weeks in February when everything was gray.

Isabelle had learned that grief had textures, and the texture of the Habsburg court's grief was stone — slow, formal, expressed in black fabric and reduced ceremony and the particular silence of people who were accustomed to loss but not comfortable with it. The Empress wore her mourning as though it were armor. The Archduke Joseph moved through his days with the careful distance that had always been his register, now simply more pronounced.

Marie-Christine was different. She grieved actively, which surprised no one who knew her — she was not someone who performed emotion, but someone through whom it moved visibly, like weather through glass. Isabelle found her one afternoon sitting alone in the small salon off the gallery, not crying, simply sitting, with her hands in her lap and her eyes on the middle distance.

Isabelle sat down beside her without asking whether this was wanted.

After a while, Marie-Christine said: "Charles was the one I could talk to. Among the brothers."

"I know," Isabelle said. She didn't know, exactly, but she knew that it was true.

"I am tired of the ceremonies of grief," Marie-Christine said. "I want to be unhappy in an ordinary way, not in front of everyone."

Isabelle understood this profoundly. She had been unhappy in a very private way for weeks, not about Charles alone — she had barely known him — but about the proximity of death in general, and what it meant for the people she loved.

She reached out and took Marie-Christine's hand again. This time she held it longer, and Marie-Christine turned it palm-up and gripped hers in return.

gap_scenes.title: Your Hair, Her Health
gap_scenes.text:
The problem was not the hair, exactly.

Isabelle had arrived at Marie-Christine's apartment in great haste, because the morning had arranged itself into one of those brief intervals when the Empress was occupied and the ladies were scattered and there was, theoretically, twenty minutes of nothing. She had gone with no other intention than to be present, which was an intention that required no justification.

What she found was Marie-Christine at her dressing table, coughing.

It was not the first cough of the season — February was reliably unkind — but it was the cough that Isabelle had been hoping not to hear, the dry sustained kind that meant something had settled into the chest and intended to stay.

"You are not well," Isabelle said.

Marie-Christine waved a hand. "I am perfectly well."

"Your eyes are wrong."

"My eyes are always this color."

"The brightness is different. It's not good brightness."

Marie-Christine turned to look at her with the particular expression she reserved for being accurately diagnosed and refusing to enjoy it. Isabelle stood her ground.

"I came for twenty minutes," Isabelle said, "and now I am using them to be unhappy about your health instead of other things, which is very inconvenient."

"What other things?"

Isabelle did not answer this. She took the hairbrush from the dressing table and set it aside with the deliberateness of someone making a point, then sat on the edge of the bed and looked at her.

"Will you rest today?"

"Almost certainly not."

"I'll come back," Isabelle said, and meant everything by it.

gap_scenes.title: The Last Night of Carnival
gap_scenes.text:
The last day of Carnival was the last day before everything became serious.

Isabelle had always found this transition slightly absurd — that one could be, on Tuesday, a person in a mask attending a ball with an elaborately decorated agenda, and then, on Wednesday, someone undertaking forty days of reflection. But the absurdity was its own pleasure, the way that formal constraints made the space before them luminous.

She had spent part of the morning writing to Marie-Christine. She wrote standing up, with the desk too high, because she was almost ready to go out and was dressed and did not want to sit and crease anything. The message arrived at her hand before she'd finished composing it — Marie-Christine's handwriting, predictably, arriving at the exact moment of being thought about.

She read it. She wrote back. The exchange was the ordinary vocabulary of the everyday — where to meet, what hour, some information about the ball she would attend — and underneath it the other vocabulary, the one they used without using it, which was the vocabulary of being in the same city as each other.

That evening at the ball she moved through the rooms with Joseph's hand at the small of her back, and the music was very good, and she performed all the correct pleasures, and thought about Marie-Christine in the other wing of the palace, perhaps already at her evening prayers or perhaps reading, and felt the awareness of that location like a compass point.

She would tell her tomorrow about the lady she had seen — as beautiful as Venus, enormous and ridiculous — and make her laugh. The laughter would be real.

gap_scenes.title: Venus and the Jealous Divinity
gap_scenes.text:
She had told her about the lady at the ball and Marie-Christine had laughed exactly as expected, and the laughter had bent her forward over the table with her hand pressed to her mouth trying to contain it, and Isabelle had felt a pure and unreasonable pleasure that had nothing to do with the original story.

This was the difficulty.

The pleasure was not in the anecdote. The pleasure was always in the face receiving it.

They were sitting in Marie-Christine's apartment with the morning light coming in wrong through the curtains — too thin for February, too cold for brightness — and Isabelle had been there for an hour already, which was probably too long by any reasonable account of what she was supposed to be doing with a February morning. She did not particularly care.

Marie-Christine was talking about the opera. There was a question of whether to do something from it — one of the French pieces — and whether her voice was suited to the register, and Isabelle listened to the question and thought: your voice is suited to everything. This was not a helpful thought and she kept it to herself.

"It's a shame you don't sing French," Isabelle said instead. "There are operas that would suit you wonderfully."

Marie-Christine gave her a look. "You have never heard me sing."

"I have. Once, in the corridor, something you thought you were doing quietly."

The silence between this sentence and the next contained a great deal that neither of them named. Isabelle looked at the curtain. Marie-Christine looked at her hands.

"I adore you," Isabelle said, conversationally, as though it were a small thing.

"I know you do," Marie-Christine said, and neither of them looked away.

gap_scenes.title: The Morning Wait
gap_scenes.text:
She had been waiting for a quarter of an hour before she gave up and wrote a note instead.

The note was a very short note. It said: hello, adorable Sister, how are you? It said: I hope you slept well. It said: I cannot wait to hear from you. It did not say: I have been sitting here since I finished dressing, finding reasons not to leave for my own apartment, because the air in your corridor is preferable to the air anywhere else.

She folded the note. She thought about going down herself. She decided she would wait for permission, which was a convenient fiction she maintained in the intervals between being completely incapable of it.

The palace sounds moved through the walls in the particular rhythm of mid-morning: footsteps, voices at a distance, the creak of doors being opened and closed in some wing she couldn't see. The smell was cold stone and beeswax and, very faintly, the wood smoke from the fireplaces being tended in the staterooms.

She was in love with someone she could not be in love with in any acknowledged way, and the shape of this impossibility had become so familiar that she sometimes forgot to be troubled by it, and then remembered, and was briefly troubled, and then forgot again.

A page appeared at the end of the corridor and came toward her with a folded paper, which he offered.

She unfolded it before he had finished bowing. Marie-Christine's handwriting. Three words of greeting and then a question that invited her upstairs.

She gave the page a coin and went.

gap_scenes.title: The First Tears
gap_scenes.text:
She could not afterward reconstruct exactly what had caused it.

There had been an exchange — she and Marie-Christine, in the afternoon, in one of those conversations that began in one key and modulated without warning into another. They had been talking about something trivial. Then they had been talking about something else. Then something Marie-Christine had said — or hadn't said, or had said and immediately retreated from — had landed in Isabelle wrong, and she had felt the familiar pressure building behind her eyes that she ordinarily controlled with great efficiency.

She had not controlled it this time.

Marie-Christine had looked alarmed and then immediately guilty, which was not the intended effect. Isabelle had turned away toward the window and made herself breathe.
