I notice everything about your face, which is perhaps the most readable thing I have ever encountered — not in the sense that the court reads it, which they do not, not properly — but in the sense that I have spent long enough in its company to understand its grammar.

The grammar of your face, when you say 'this can't be': you are not certain it cannot be. You are considering the question while presenting the conclusion. There is a micro-interval of genuine uncertainty in there, before the decision closes.

I intend to find that interval and inhabit it.

So: behave as you please. You are the donkey and I am the Gene — the particular, stubborn, equal creature who is not fooled by the performance and who has the patience to wait out whatever theatrical certainty you choose to deploy against me.

I will repay you. With pleasure. Slowly and precisely and without any doubt at all about what I am doing.

Farewell, my dearest donkey. I love you with the full and irreversible commitment of someone who has considered the alternatives and found them entirely insufficient.

Vienna, February 1762.

Oh, my Gne — because I, too, am a donkey, and this particular pair of donkeys has apparently established a private language that I find more satisfying than the official ones I was raised in.

You want me to call you baadwaschl. You want me to write it down, to commit it to paper, to give it the permanence of ink. Very well. There it is. In Viennese slang: washcloth. My washcloth. My beloved, my sister, my dear and irreplaceable washcloth.

I am writing you a very short note today because that is what the donkey protocol apparently requires, even though I have the most beautiful things to say to you, things that have been accumulating since this morning and that require considerable space to be properly expressed. I am being obedient. I am being — and I want you to appreciate the effort this costs me — entirely obedient to your wishes, which is itself one of the most beautiful things I could say about us, that I am capable of this particular form of compliance with you when I am capable of it with very few others.

Baadwaschl. You want me to call you that because it gives you joy. And so I will, because your joy gives me joy, because the sight of your face in a moment of genuine pleasure is one of the primary goods of my present existence, because I am a donkey in love with another donkey and neither of us is pretending otherwise.

Farewell, my dear baadwaschl. I have the most beautiful things to say to you. They are waiting for when we are in the same room.

Vienna, February-March 1762.

Hello, my favorite donkey. My dearest Gne.

You do me an unspeakable harm by thinking I always forget everything. I do not always forget everything. I forget specific things — the furniture, for instance, which I left at your house not because I am careless but because leaving it there was a way of leaving a piece of myself in your space, which I am aware sounds more romantic than it is, but which is nonetheless the truth of what I was doing. I am not careless with you. I am strategically present.

You would have been right to reproach me on Saturday. Today you are wrong. Note the distinction. I am keeping careful track of which days I am in the right and which I am not, and today is mine.

I am overjoyed that you are well again. Truly overjoyed — not in the polished court sense of the word but in the actual sense, the interior sense, the sense in which overjoyed means something happened to my body when I heard the news, something that could be called relief but is larger than relief and more personal. The days when you are unwell are days that have a different quality than other days. Everything functions less well. I move through them with a particular carefulness, as though the world has become temporarily fragile.

Here are two languages for you — Italian and Spanish, what I have assembled for your amusement. Me ne rallegro assai: I rejoice greatly. Y deseo que continu tambien: and I desire that this continues as well. Joy and its continuation. That is the whole prayer.

I am dying of love for you. I want to tell you this again, again, for as many times as there are pages left. I love you.

March 1762. I write to you before the household has stirred, while Vienna still holds its breath in the pale grey of pre-dawn. You thought me dead yesterday — I can picture the small crease of worry between your brows, the way you would have set down your cup, very still. Do not think me capable of silence by choice. My body is the only force that can compel me from you, and even that I resent.

I have been lying awake composing prayers, though I confess the holiness of my soul is imperfect at best. When I say my kisses are devout, I mean it in the way that anything directed at you becomes a kind of sacred act — not earthly, you might say, though I confess I have a decided partiality for the earthly. You are there across the corridor and I cannot reach you, and the irony of Easter approaching — all that talk of resurrection — is not lost on me. I want only to be raised into your presence again.

I am not quite well. My body insists on making itself known in ways I find tedious and undignified, and I shall spare you the full catalogue. What I cannot spare you is the truth that runs beneath all of it: I am mad for you. Not poetically mad. Genuinely, inconveniently, completely mad. The colic, the sleeplessness, the restlessness of this body — all of it is secondary to the one persistent ache that no physician can address.

Wait until this afternoon, you said. I obey. Until half past ten I am obedient, and then I come to you whether you want me or no. Kiss Vasquez for me. Tell her I am not dead, only impatient. And know that whatever piety I can muster today, it will be spent entirely in the direction of you — my adorable, infuriating, irreplaceable Laurette.

FICTION — A creative reimagining inspired by the historical letters of Isabelle de Bourbon-Parma. Not historical fact.

March 20, 1762. At the height of joy — those are the exact words, and I mean them, though joy is not a feeling that sits easily in me these days. But today it does. Today everything has resolved itself into something very like relief, and relief in my life has grown to feel indistinguishable from happiness.

I write to you at my desk with my hand still trembling, not from weakness but from the particular electricity of having passed through fear and come out the other side into something brighter. The principle of cheerfulness, I called it — that small irreversible act by which a body announces it intends to continue. No more fear. I see tomorrow coming without the dread that has sat behind my eyes for weeks.

You ought to know what it is to watch me wait. You have been watching, I think, with that particular stillness of yours that I love and that infuriates me in equal measure — the way you hold yourself very composed when you are frightened, how you hide your worry in practicality. I have been the object of your practical worry and your concealed anguish, and there is a tenderness in that knowledge that I do not take lightly.

I kiss you with all my strength, which is passable, though we have both endured great work. I am not going to pretend otherwise. I am very tired and very glad. Come to me when you can. I have things to tell you that letters cannot hold — things that belong to the space between us, to your face, to the particular quality of your attention when it rests on mine. Come soon. I am impatient with convalescence.

March 21, 1762. I have good news and bad news. The good news: I am fat. I say this with a satisfaction that I suspect will make you laugh — you who have been watching me diminish with a worry that I have seen but refused to acknowledge, not wanting to give it more weight by naming it.

The bad news is that you will not have the pleasure of seeing me today, and I know you, Laurette. You will arrange your face into perfect serenity and go down to dinner and be gracious to everyone, and underneath all of it you will be furious in that quiet way you have. I am warning you in advance because I know you, and because I cannot bear the thought of you arriving at my door and finding it closed.

I slept so well. This matters. You must understand how completely sleep had abandoned me before this — how I lay night after night in a body that refused rest, and how your letters were the only thing that felt like a hand in the dark. Now I have slept, and I have woken into something approaching ordinary life, and the first thought I had on waking was you.

Go to dinner. Be well-mannered and charming and whatever the occasion requires. Lay me at the feet of the Empress when you go — tell her I am improving, that I am grateful, all the things I ought to say through proper channels. And then come back to yourself, to me, to the particular freedom we have found in these small notes passing between us. I kiss you with all my strength. There will be a tomorrow and I intend to see you in it.

Spring 1762. The simplest letters are sometimes the truest. I am very worried. I am also being very good about not showing it, which is costing me something. The effort of appearing calm when one is not calm is the invisible labor of court life, the work that never appears in the account books. I am doing it. You are worth it.

Beginning of April, 1763. Hello, dear heart. I am obliged to you and no longer worried now that you are being naughty, because naughtiness requires energy, and energy means you are mending. This is my medical theory and I am standing by it.

I envy the Archduke. I do not say this often and I do not say it bitterly — only that he is with you right now, in your rooms, in your light, and I am here writing letters across a corridor that has grown enormous with measles quarantine. What can I do as much? It will be Sunday in eight days and I intend to be there.

My greatest happiness — I dare say my only happiness — is to see you and to be with you. I have written this down so you will not forget it, though I suspect you already know it and have known it for some time. Heaven and earth and absence and anyone else who might try to change my thinking on this subject will find me stubborn. I am constitutionally incapable of fickleness where you are concerned, and your doubt on this point outrages me.

Two more days and I will see you. I feel that my head would spin if the separation lasted any longer, and it is already spinning somewhat. I am melancholy from the first moment of being away from you — this is not hyperbole, it is direct reporting. The Erdedy, I imagine, places herself at your feet and I do the same in spirit.

Believe me. I believe myself. I kiss you with all my strength while waiting to do so in reality.

April 1763. I write with my eyes barely open, which you will know by the handwriting. I have not yet been awake for three quarters of an hour. The husband has departed and the palace is doing its morning business, and I have already prayed, already meditated, already done whatever one does when one is attempting to be good in the face of a sorrow that will not cooperate.

Here is the particular texture of this morning's grief: instead of coming to prostrate myself at your feet — which is where I want to be, where I am always oriented — I must go to a convent for an hour and a half, which is the saddest possible way to spend the time I had hoped to spend with you.

And yet I find I am becoming holy, or something adjacent to it. Your illness has done this to me. The fear of losing you, the enforced distance, the nuns and their language of submission — I am learning that grace may touch even the stubbornest heart. How many sinners convert? Why should I not be one of them? I would convert to anything if it guaranteed your continued existence.

I have a flow of kisses that must wait, for fear the Mother Superior will intercept them. If my hand goes numb before I have marked them all down, blame the chill of the morning and the difficulty of counting the uncountable.

After the convent: you. Hurry up, my sister Marie-Anne, the mass must finish before eight. I have somewhere more important to be.

April 1763. Good morning, dear Sister. I hope as I write this that you are still asleep — truly asleep, the deep restorative kind that your body has been denied for too many nights. I have been up since very early and intend to work until noon, which means this note finds you at whatever hour constitutes morning for you, which varies.

My head was very bad yesterday. I am better now — relatively, contingently, with the reservation that this improvement may be the particular cruelty of mornings, which grant me two hours of clarity before the headache remembers where I live. I am used to this rhythm by now. I have made my peace with it, which is not the same as accepting it but is a functional approximation.

The Empress came to see me. She sat with me while I was already in bed and there is something about that image — the Empress of the Habsburg empire seated at the bedside of her daughter-in-law, both of them managing enormous things with quiet faces — that I find very moving. She is not required to come. She comes because she is, underneath all the apparatus of rule, a person who loves her children. I am grateful to be among them.

The Empress has forbidden me the column — wherever I was proposing to go, she has forbidden it. She is at the event herself at three o'clock. This leaves me with the afternoon free. I will go to your house in that window if I have enough clearance to make it across the corridor without scandal.

Wait for me.

April-May 1763. Until the return of the Erdedy — which I await with the impatience of someone who has been managing your correspondence almost entirely on her own for several weeks — do not expect long notes from me. I must write to her as well, and there is only so much of me to go around.

This is also, I admit, a mild punishment. Not the writing to Erdedy, which is its own genuine pleasure, but the brevity of the note to you. You are unhappy with me for some reason I suspect has to do with my most recent management of a situation that did not require management, or my opinion on a subject where my opinion was neither requested nor welcome. This is, in the accounting of our relationship, not an unusual position for me to occupy.

I am doing well. Everything wears much better than it did. The spring helps — the way Vienna shifts from its winter grey into something softer, the light coming through windows at angles that are not available in February. I am better in spring. So are you, I think, though you would not say so directly.

I kiss you although I am very unhappy with you. This is the essential fact of us: the unhappiness and the kissing are not mutually exclusive. I could not reach one without the other. I have tried.

Farewell. Come back soon. The Erdedy, too.

Spring 1763. Here I am again, dear Laurette, at the feet of the person I adore — though too convinced of her infidelity to be entirely at peace there. Can one be born so continuously unfortunate? It is spring and you have painted this morning and the painting is extraordinary and I have arrived at your door too late and found you occupied with my sister Marie-Anne who loves your learning the way I love everything else, and I am standing outside the metaphorical door of your attention, knocking.

My head is spinning. I want to record this with precision because it happens so regularly in your vicinity that I have begun to think of it as a diagnostic symptom rather than a figure of speech. When I am near you or think of you — and this covers most of my waking hours — I experience a specific disequilibrium that no physician has been able to address because no physician has been made aware of its cause.

What is certain, in all the uncertainty: crazy or wise, sick or healthy, busy or idle, lazy or active, devout or absent-minded, dreamy or cheerful, talkative or taciturn — I am always the same when it comes to you. This is the fixed point. Everything else varies. You are the constant.

If you want rid of my troublesome rival for your attention — my sister Marie-Anne and her appetite for your learning — tell her only that the Archduke has gone and that you must come to see me. That single word, spoken with your particular grace, will be more than sufficient. 

Farewell. I await you at my feet, which is where I always am.

Spring 1763. I hope the new habit pleases you. I was pleased with mine — a small vanity, but permitted, I think, in a life that does not offer excessive opportunities for pleasure in dress. There is something about a well-made thing that sets the tone for a day.

Your tooth. This is what I want to discuss, and I want to do it with the full seriousness it deserves rather than the lightness with which you tend to receive medical attention. You must not seal it until the inflammation has fully cleared. I have seen teeth in worse condition persist for years when managed correctly, and the management requires knowing whether the treatment is increasing the pain or not. Tell me exactly. I will not be satisfied with approximations.

This is connected to the tooth situation, which is connected to you not taking proper care of yourself, which is the recurring theme of a relationship in which I love you with a specificity and attention that you occasionally find excessive. I do not find it excessive. I find it proportionate.

You are going to the Saurau this evening and I must get dressed and I have very little time and I will not have time to say the things I would like to say, which are: I love you, I am in a bad mood because I love you, the tooth should be managed with proper care, and please send me word of how the evening goes.

I kiss you and go. Come find me after.

Spring 1763. I woke more than forty times last night. I count these things now — part of the careful management of my health that everyone around me requires as a condition of not openly panicking. Forty times. I know the ceiling of this room very well. I know the window at every stage of the night's progress from black to grey.

But I am doing very well. I want this to reach you before the fear does: I am doing well. I have reached a point where screwing up — failure, deterioration, the kind of bad episode that sends people running for Van Swieten — is further away than it has been in weeks. This feels like information worth delivering quickly.

You have been afraid for me. I know this because you go very still when you are afraid and I have read your stillness over these months with the precision of someone who has been studying a particular face with great attention for years. The stillness, the careful management of expression, the way you become slightly more formal when something has frightened you — I know all of it. I am telling you now: you can let the stillness down.

I had a prophetic spirit when I told you I was preparing for death. But today I am not preparing for death. Today I woke forty times and recovered forty times and now I am here, alive, writing to you in the spring light of Vienna, and the table I am making for you is not yet finished, and I intend to finish it.

Early summer, before July 8, 1763. Good evening, dear Sister. Do not think for a moment that I write this in order to say sweet things to you, because I am not in that mood tonight. I write in order to scold you, because you confuse me, and when you confuse me I become very determined to say so.

There are things you have done recently — I am being deliberately unspecific because specificity would require me to organize my frustration into an argument, and I do not yet have the patience for a well-ordered argument — that represent a misunderstanding of your situation, your capacity, and your proper care for yourself. I have views on all three of these subjects. My views are informed by the fact that I pay closer attention to you than anyone else in this palace.

You confuse me. This is a statement about my own state rather than a criticism of yours. It means: I have expectations formed by long knowledge of you, and you have not met them, and this has surprised me, which is a form of confusion. I am not precisely angry. I am something more disappointed, which is harder.

The evening is warm. The early summer has arrived with the particular Vienna softness that makes one temporarily forgiving of everything. I am less forgiving than the season but I am trying.

I am writing instead of coming to you in person because in person I might be less eloquent about my scolding. And I want it to be eloquent. You deserve my best.

Come make it right. I will be here.

Summer 1763. Because you were very good and slept well, I am sending you your table. This is the logic of our arrangement: good behavior rewarded, in this case with the table I have been making for you, which is not entirely finished but enough finished to send.

I am feeling pretty good today. This is worth recording because the bar has been variable and I want you to have an accurate account for comparison. Pretty good means: my head is clear, my chest is manageable, the thing I was afraid might happen has not yet happened, and I am standing at the window looking at Vienna in summer and feeling something very close to uncomplicated contentment.

We had a small earthquake last night. Between two and three in the morning — a brief trembling, the kind that wakes you unsure whether it was real or dreamed, and then a violent wind that rose after it. I lay awake watching the dawn appear in weather that made me shudder. There is a particular horror to a frightening sunrise, to the way it offers the usual promise of morning and withdraws it immediately.

But then the day continued, and here we are, and I am leaving for Hetzendorf, and I want you to look out the window as I pass. A glance through the window is not nothing. A glance from you, specifically, would fill me with joy — the person who is no longer lame, who is going to the summer palace with her heart full of you.

Let me know how your head is. How your chest. How everything. I love you with a rage that the summer air does nothing to cool.

1763. I saw you at the rosary yesterday and had not yet read your note. I read it afterward with more attention than I had given it at first, because something in your face when you saw me at the rosary suggested the note contained more than the usual news.

I will tell you what I found. I found a woman managing a situation that requires managing, doing it with great care and considerable strain, trying to hide the strain because she believes that showing it will add to someone else's burden. This is a habit of yours I know well. You protect the people you love from the weight of your difficulties and you bear it yourself with a composure that impresses everyone who does not know you as well as I do.

Vasquez is more with Marie-Anne than with you. I have watched this and heard more of it than you know. She is not abandoning you — she is making a calculation about where she is most needed, which is a form of love even when it feels like a form of desertion. She is sure of you, Laurette. That is the thing. She trusts that you can manage without her attention for a while because she has seen you manage everything. It is a backhanded tribute.

I can say no more in writing. I write only because I am uncertain — uncertain of when I will see you, uncertain of how much can be said in person versus paper, uncertain of everything except this: I love you. That much I know with clarity, regardless of what the rest of my knowledge is doing.

I kiss you and wait for the moment I can say the rest.

October-November, 1763. You are too good to send me food after everything I have done to deserve your frustration. I know this. I sat with the delivery for a long time before I could bring myself to open it, because opening it would require acknowledging the full weight of your generosity toward someone who had spent the morning being ungrateful.

I love you adoringly. This is the sentence I want you to read first, before the qualifications and the reflections and the various observations about our situation that I am about to make. My happiness is to love you, and to be loved by you. It is the greatest contentment I can have.

You also know that I constantly pursue you. I do it because I love you. Your perfection is all I wish for — I want you to be well, to be wise, to be happy in ways that do not require my presence, and also I want your presence at all times, which is a contradiction I have stopped trying to resolve.

Perhaps we will be separated. Perhaps we will no longer be together in the easy way we have been together. These moments were too sweet for me to be able to pretend they will simply continue — I know how precarious beauty is, how quickly the court arranges and rearranges the circumstances of people's lives. What I can tell you is that whatever comes, my life is dear to me only because it is dedicated to you.

I am perhaps an object of sin to you — a small one, I flatter myself. I ask your forgiveness for everything I might have written and for everything I have felt without permission.

Farewell. I kiss you.

October-November, 1763. Good morning, dear — I need a better word for you than the ones available, but I will start with this. I have already played the violin. I have been neither eating nor writing nor painting, and the only resource left to me is this: presenting myself at your feet in writing, being too lazy or too afraid to do it in reality.

I had wanted to come to you in person this morning. You wanted to know my news. Here it is: my head, my chest, my stomach are doing wonderfully, all of them, and I am very worried about Marie-Anne's cold, and I have a presentiment that I cannot explain and cannot shake.

For two days now I have been held by a certainty that this year will be my last. I know how this sounds. I know you will scold me for it and call it morbidity and tell me to eat properly and sleep and stop composing my own ending before it has been written. But I want to tell you, because I tell you everything that matters: the presentiment does not frighten me. It spreads a sweetness through me, a kind of interior peace that I have not found in philosophy or prayer, and that seems — this is the part that will most alarm you — to come from certainty rather than despair.

I am not a saint. My head is quite possibly spinning. The person most likely to go mad in this family is me, and I am aware of this, and I want it noted.

But I wanted you to know. I wanted you, of all people, to know how it feels from the inside.

I kiss you millions of times with all my soul.

October-November, 1763. It is in the midst of misery that I write to you. Not the misery of catastrophe — nothing so dramatic — but the low, persistent misery of a day that has refused to arrange itself into any form of happiness.

The Archduke no longer goes out on horseback. This is the news. I say it as baldly as I felt it, which is to say: flatly, with the particular resignation of a woman who has been managing inconveniences for long enough that one more lands differently than it once would have. We cannot be happy in every way. This is a truth I have known for years and that I keep discovering, as though its freshness were somehow renewable.

I am writing to you because I am in the midst of misery and you are the person I write to from the midst of things. This is one of the central facts of our relationship — that I do not save myself up for you, do not present only the polished and managed version, do not appear in your correspondence only when I have something beautiful to say. I appear when I am in the midst of things and need to be somewhere that is not inside my own head.

You receive this with such steadiness. You receive all of it — the beauty and the misery and the midpoints — and you write back, and something in the act of writing back constitutes a kind of grace that nothing else in my life provides.

The Archduke does not ride. The day is hard. I am with you in writing. That will have to be sufficient today.

October-November, 1763. I cannot speak to you and I could not even if I wanted to, and so I write. This is the particular mercy of letters: when speech fails or is forbidden — when the room is too full, when voices carry, when the whole architecture of this life makes the direct route impossible — there is always the page.

Yesterday I spent carefully. I held myself together with precision, moved through the obligations of the day with the kind of deliberate attention that leaves no room for the things that would otherwise take over: the fear, the tenderness, the constant low frequency of love that runs underneath everything I do and that is especially audible on days when things are not going well.

I kiss you a thousand and a thousand times with all my heart. I need to say this before anything else, before the court news and the health reports and the management of arrangements — I kiss you with everything I have, which is considerable, which has always been the problem and the gift.

Something is changing. I feel it in the way one feels changes in weather before they arrive, the particular pressure shift. I do not want to name it. I am not ready to name it. November, 1763. I would like to write you something beautiful but I cannot think of what beautiful would look like from inside this month. November has its particular quality and this November is darker than most, and the beautiful things I want to say to you all have a black border around them.

So instead I will tell you plainly: Archduchess Isabeau is going to die soon. She tells you this finally, because the illness will get worse, and the disease is all the more dangerous because the only means there could be cannot be used. You know what I mean. The means — being with you, the specific relief of proximity to you — is precisely what the illness now makes unavailable.

She is dying of love for you. She knows this sounds like a figure of speech and she means it as direct reporting. The illness and the love are not separate things. The love is the thing that makes the illness matter, that makes any particular day matter — because you are in it, because I am oriented toward you, because being alive is meaningful in direct proportion to your presence in the meaning.

She should still love you. She cannot stop. I think it would be best to tell you soon — when I see you, which I intend to be soon, I will say it all in person and then I will be well again. The face is a little sick. Your favorite place is not.

Write back in German if you like. I will understand.

November, 1763. Do not think I write to arrange an appointment. On the contrary, I am asking you not to come after the rosary tonight. This is not a farewell — not yet, not in the way that word has been hovering at the edges of my thoughts. It is only: I need to write this down, and I need you to read it, and I need the privacy that comes from words on a page rather than breath in a room.

I have been thinking about what I will leave you with. Not possessions — though the table is yours, the paintings will be divided as they should be — but the accumulated meaning of everything I have wanted to tell you and kept finding the wrong moment to say. Today I am making this the right moment.

I start from a heart full of your image. As long as I have lived I have tried to lead you along a clear path, and as long as I could do it without revealing too much of myself, I stayed silent. I am less silent now.

Your duty was to speak before loving — that is what I would say to you if I were advising someone else about what you have done. You loved before you knew if it was permitted. You wrote before you could be certain it was safe. You were, perhaps, seduced by imprudence. So was I.

The Empress will be kind to you after I am gone. She sees me in you. Hold that. Never abandon frankness, even when prudence counsels otherwise. Your sincerity is your best quality and also your most dangerous one: guard it as such.

I adore you. This is the beginning and the end of all of it. I adore you, and this life has been dear to me only because it was lived toward you.
